title: Homework Problems
text:
Write a truth table for “(not \(P\)) and (not \(Q\))”. This could be called a “neither nor” truth table. Using that, infer a truth table for “NOT ((not \(P\)) and (not \(Q\)))”. This could be called, awkwardly, a truth table for “not neither nor”. It should exactly match a more familiar table. Which one?



For each logical critique, identify whether it is primarily a syntax issue or a semantic issue.

Your parentheses don’t match.
Your premise is usually true but not always true.
Your first premise uses the word “political” with one meaning, but your second premise uses the word “political” with a slightly different meaning.
The form of the argument is “if \(P\) then \(Q\). Moreover \(Q\). Therefore \(P\).” This is not a valid argument structure.
Your handwriting is messy.
Your conclusion is a generalization, but I know a specific exception. So something in your argument has to be wrong.




If \(P\) is an assertion, does \(\neg \neg P\) have the same meaning as \(P\)? Explain.



Consider this algebraic proof:
\[
\begin{align}
x^2 = 3x-2\\
x^2 -3x + 2 = 0\\
(x-2)(x-1) = 0\\
x-2 = 0  \,\,\underline{\hspace{1in}}\,\, x-1 = 0\\
x = 2  \,\,\underline{\hspace{1in}}\,\, x = 1\\
\end{align}
\]

The blank spaces represent the word “or” or “and”. Which is most appropriate, and why?
If this is a direct proof of something, what does it establish?

If \(x^2 = 3x-2\) then \(x\) is 2 and/or 1.

The numbers \(1\) and \(2\) are solutions to the equation \(x^2 = 3x-2\)
\(x\) is equal to both \(1\) and \(2\).
Algebra is awesome.

Is the larger argument correct for all \(x\), for some certain \(x\), or for only \(x=1\) or \(x=2\)?




Let \(f(x) = \frac{x}{|x|}\), a function defined only for nonzero inputs \(x\). Prove that for all nonzero \(x\), \(f(x) = \pm 1\), using a proof structure that works by cases.



Consider the following proof:

Let \(\varepsilon\) be the smallest positive real number. Then \(0 < \varepsilon\). Dividing both sides of this equation by \(2\), we have \(0 < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\). Adding \(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\) to both sides, we have \(\frac{\varepsilon}{2} < \varepsilon\). We have shown that \(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\) is positive and smaller than \(\varepsilon\), but this is directly at odds with the nature (first sentence) of \(\varepsilon\).


What is an appropriate conclusion of the proof?

\(\frac{\varepsilon}{2} < \varepsilon\)
There must be an algebraic mistake.
There is no smallest positive real number.
There may be a smallest positive real number, but it isn’t \(\varepsilon\)
\(\varepsilon\) is the smallest positive real number but there is a smaller positive real number, namely \(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\)

What proof structure is used above? (i.e., direct, contrapositive, contradiction, etc)?




Consider the following joke argument:

If the Earth were flat, then in the past thousands of years, cats would have knocked everything off the edge by now. They haven’t done so, so the Earth isn’t flat.


Is this an argument by contradiction, by contrapositive, or by modus tollens? Explain.




Prove that the the sum of any two even integers is even. Interpret “even” to mean double some integer. Structure your proof correctly to prove a universal statement.



Prove that for any \(n\), \(n^3-n\) is divisible by \(3\). I suggest that you divide the problem into three cases, based on the fact that any number can be written \(3k\) or \(3k+1\) or \(3k+2\).



Prove that \(A \cap (B \cup C) \subseteq
(A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\). The goal is to reason explicitly from the arbitrary particular to the general. Remember that any subset statement is a generalization about all elements of one set.



Prove that for all integers \(n\), \(n^2+n\) is even.



Interpret and prove the statement below. You should pay careful attention to structure of proof. \[ \forall x \enspace \forall y \enspace (x \neq y \to \exists z \enspace (x<z<y \lor y <z<x)) \]

text:
2.1 I order a sub with nothing on it.
Here \(A\) is an arbitary set and \(\emptyset\) is the empty set.

Is the statement “\(\forall x (x \in \emptyset \to x \in A)\)” true or false? Explain.
Rewrite the statement (without changing its meaning) so that it uses the subset “\(\subseteq\)” symbol.

title: Homework Problems
text:
2.2 Typing practice
Let \(f\) be a function from \({\mathbb R}\) to \({\mathbb R}\) by the formula \(f(x) = x^4+1\). Let \(A\) be the set \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7\}\) and let \(B\) be the set \(\{7,8,9,10\}\). What is the type of each of the mathematical objects below? Your answer in each case should be “number”, “function”, “truth value”, “set”, etc.

\(A \cap B\)
\(A \cup B\)
\(\{A,B\}\)
\(\emptyset = A\)
\({\mathbb R}\)
The image of \(f\)
\(x\)
\(f(x)\)
\(f\)
\(f(7)\)
\(f(2) = f(-2)\)

Based on the set-theoretical descriptions of \(0\), \(1\), and \(2\) from section 3.2, what are \(3\) and \(4\)? Writing these sets completely (not using the notation \(\emptyset\)), how many curly braces are needed to represent each of \(0\), \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), and \(4\)?

A function \(f\) has domain \(\{1,2,3\}\) and range \({\mathbb R}\). What are the possibilities for the image of \(f\)?

text:

Let \(f:{\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R}\) by \(f(x) = x^2+1\) and let \(g:{\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R}\) by \(g(t) = t^2+1\).

True or False: \(f(x)=g(x)\)

Find a function \(g\) which is a right inverse of \(f\).

title: Homework Problems
text:

Let \(h:{\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R}\) by \(h(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 3x - 1\). Prove that \(h\) is surjective. (Hint: Although there might be another way, I expect that factoring the polynomial will be enormously useful!)

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.8 Bijective via inverse.
Let \(f:{\mathbb R} \to {\mathbb R}\) by \(f(x) = 7x+2\). Find an inverse function, then prove it’s an inverse function, then infer that \(f\) is a bijection.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.9 Bijection via inverse
Let \(f:{\mathbb Z}_{11} \to {\mathbb Z}_{11}\) by \(f(x) = 3x\). For example \(f(5) = 15 = 4\). Find an inverse function \(g:{\mathbb Z}_{11} \to {\mathbb Z}_{11}\). (A simple multiplication formula is possible.) Prove that they are inverse functions, and infer that \(f\) is a bijection.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.10 Functions to 2
Let \(X\) be a set. Let \(\mathscr{P}(X)\) be its power set, and let \(2^X\) be the set of all functions \(f: X \to \{0,1\}\). 1. Provide a function \(h:\mathscr{P}(X) \to 2^X\). 2. Provide a function \(k:2^X \to h:\mathscr{P}(X)\). 3. Prove that \(h\) and \(k\) are inverse functions.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.11 A surprise injection
Find an injection from \({\mathbb N} \times {\mathbb N}\) to \({\mathbb N}\). Prove that it is an injection.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.12 There is no surjectivity.
Some say that if a function is truly nothing more than a set of ordered (input/output) pairs, then surjectivity is meaningless. Explain.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.13 Induction? Hard to say.
Explain in your own words why the principle of mathematical induction is problematic within a simple number theory in which the only mathematical objects of relevance are natural numbers.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.14 Powers of 2 equivalence
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be natural numbers, we write \(x \sim y\) to mean \(y/x\) is a power of \(2\). (Powers of \(2\) are numbers \(2^n\) for all \(n \in {\mathbb Z}\), including \(1\), \(1/2\), etc.) Prove that \(x \sim y\) is an equivalence relation.

title: Homework Problems
text:
3.15 Ordering tasks.
A complex to-do list contains many tasks. We use variables \(x\) and \(y\) to range over the tasks themselves. For example, \(x=\)(repair faucet) and \(y=\)(rake leaves). Some tasks have interdependencies. We write \(x \le y\) to mean \(x=y\) or \(x\) must be completed before \(y\) can begin. For example (buy brake light replacement) \(\le\) (install brake light replacement). Discuss each of the five order axioms in this context. Which are true? Is this system a partial order? total order? well order?

2 Course Information
Credit Hours: 3
Schedule: Monday and Wednesday, 2:30-3:45
Prerequisites: Formally, 451 and permission. Informally, 671 and 691 are expected.
Required textbooks/materials: Instructor notes provided. You may also find it useful to read Functions of One Complex Variable I, 2nd ed. by Conway (optional).
Course Description: This is a first course in complex analysis. We will cover the complex number system, metric topology, analytic functions, power series, path integration, and Cauchy’s residue theorem.

text:

We will have two mid-semester exams during the semester and a final exam at the end.

text:
4 Appendices

4.1 AI Policy:
Students are encouraged to leverage AI tools, such as Jupyter with code completion features or chatbots for learning help, to enhance their understanding of mathematical concepts and streamline computational tasks. All interactions with AI systems are consultations with an external source, just like a book or another person. Copying the work of an AI system and submitting it as ones own, even with some changes, is a form of plagiarism. Calling on AI for solutions to assigned problems is cheating, for the same reason that hiring your Mom to do your homework is cheating.


4.2 Accommodative Services
Students who need accommodations to complete the requirements and expectations of this course because of a disability should contact the Office of Accommodative Services (136 Sisson Hall, (315) 267-2590, oas@potsdam.edu) or complete their request by filling out the New Student Accommodation Request Form. Please note that accommodations are generally not provided retroactively so timely contact with the Office of Accommodative Services is important. Students registered with the Office of Accommodative Services (OAS) should use the Accommodate Portal to submit their “Semester Request” (Letter of Accommodation) every semester. This letter informs faculty of potential course access and accommodations that might be necessary and reasonable. Further conversation with OAS, faculty, and the student may be warranted to ensure reasonable accommodations.


4.3 Counseling Services
As a student at SUNY Potsdam, you may encounter various stressors that can affect your learning and academic performance. The College Counseling Center (CCC) offers a range of resources to support students in their mental health, social well-being, and overall academic experience. Students seeking to speak with a licensed mental health professional can access free services through the SUNY Potsdam Counseling Center. To connect with our services, please call 315-267-2330, email counseling@potsdam.edu, or visit us at Van Housen 131.


4.4 Disruptive Student Policy
In order to maintain a fair, just, and safe College community environment, students are subject to SUNY Potsdam College regulations and are expected to abide by the Potsdam Pledge, the SUNY Potsdam Academic Catalog, and the Student Community Rights and Responsibilities (the Student Code of Conduct). Anyone who disrupts the academic learning environment (e.g., classrooms, labs, office hours, online platforms, emails, or other virtual communications) will be asked to leave for the day. Disruptions may include, but are not limited to, interrupting/speaking over other people, excessive use of foul or abusive or derogatory language, and repeated getting up/leaving/returning behavior. Students who exhibit aggressive/violent behavior in or out of classrooms will be asked to immediately leave. Disruptive students may be subject to disciplinary action, potentially including administrative removal from the course.


4.5 Food Insecurity
The Prometheus Alumni Food Pantry is in 119 Barrington Student Union. The hours of operation can be found on their Facebook page or Get Involved. An Initial Intake is required 3 of all visitors. Additionally, if you are living off campus and in need of supplemental food assistance, you may be eligible for SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits. To determine eligibility and to enroll, you can visit mybenefits.ny.gov or call Maximizing Independent Living Choices (MILC) at 315-764-9442 x405. The campus has a registered dietician to assist you; you can contact them through the Student Health Services student portal on BearPaws. If you have questions on any of these services or need further assistance, reach out to the Bear CARE Program.


4.6 Land Acknowledgement
We acknowledge with respect the Mohawk Nation, the Indigenous people on whose ancestral lands SUNY Potsdam now stands. We are reminded by our presence here that we have the duty to live in harmony with one another and with all of creation. We are deeply grateful to the families and communities who care for this beautiful place. Beginning with colonization and continuing for centuries the Haudenosaunee Peoples have been dispossessed of most of their ancestral lands by the actions of individuals and institutions. We acknowledge our responsibility to understand and respond to those actions and to commit to working together to honor our past and build our future with truth. For more information on Land Acknowledgements, see Land_Acknowledgement at illuminative.org


4.7 Success Statement
Success in this course depends heavily on your personal health and wellbeing. Recognize that stress is an expected part of the college experience, and it often can be compounded by unexpected setbacks or life changes outside the classroom. I strongly encourage you to reframe challenges as an unavoidable pathway to success. Reflect on your role in taking care of yourself throughout the term, before the demands of exams and projects reach their peak. Please feel free to reach out to me about any difficulty you may be having that may impact your performance in your courses or campus life as soon as it occurs and before it becomes too overwhelming. In addition, I strongly encourage you to contact the many other support services on campus that stand ready to assist you including the Counseling Center & the Case Manager, Student Health Services, Accommodative Services, and your academic advisor.


4.8 Student Support
Every student in this class is a valued individual. If you are struggling with issues outside of the classroom, please know that there are professionals both on and off campus who can assist you. If you need immediate assistance, please contact our campus Counseling Center (with free counseling) at (315) 267-2330 or visit their website. Links to other resources are provided below: • Title IX Coordinator, Van Housen Extension 392, (315) 267-2516, • Bias Incident Reporting • Center for Diversity, 223 Sisson Hall, (315) 267-2184 • University Police, Van Housen Extension, (315) 267-2222 (number for non-emergencies; for an emergency please dial 911) • Student Conduct and Community Standards, 208 Barrington Student Union, • Reachout (24-hour crisis hotline), (315) 265-2422 • Renewal House (for victims of domestic violence), SUNY Potsdam Campus Office: Van Housen Extension 390 (open Wednesdays, 9-5:00), (315) 379-9845 (24-hour crisis hotline), Renewalhouse_campus@Verizon.net • Career Services, Lougheed Learning Commons
And please: if you see something, say something. If you see that someone that you care about is struggling, please encourage them to seek help. If they are unwilling to do so, Care Enough to Call has guidelines on whom to contact. Everyone has the responsibility of creating a college climate of compassion.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
2.1 Constructions of \({\mathbb C}\)
The set of complex numbers \({\mathbb C}\) is defined by accepting \(\sqrt{-1}\), usually written \(i\), into the community of numbers. Once we accept \(\sqrt{-1}\), we have to accept arithmetical combinations which involve it, such as \(5+6\sqrt{-1}\), usually written \(5+6i\). We have to accept division by \(i\), which fortunately is the same as multiplication by \(-i\). (Since \(-i\cdot i=1\), the reciprocal of \(i\) is \(-i\).) It turns out that general combinations of the form \(a+bi\) are “enough” in the sense that for any two of them we can identify a sum, difference, product, or quotient also of the form \(a+bi\).
We therefore wish to define \({\mathbb C}\) to be “only” the set of numbers \(a+bi\). But in order to do so, we need to give an account of what \(a+bi\) represents. Some authors define \({\mathbb C}\) to be the set of “formal sums” \(a+bi\). This seems to avoid, rather than answer, the basic question (“What does \(a+bi\) mean?”) by defining “\(a+bi\)” to be a form representing its own form. It leaves many questions unanswered: Is \(3+1i\) identical with \(3+i\)? or \(1+2+i\)? or \(i+3\)? We feel these should be the same, but they differ in form. If \({\mathbb C}\) is defined to be a set of forms, these things should be unequal! Quite generally, to define a thing as a “formal” [form] is to intentionally confuse its nature with its method of expression, in order to avoid the real work of describing its nature. We can do much better:

Definition 1 \({\mathbb C}\) is defined to be the set of ordered pairs \((a,b)\): \[{\mathbb C} \equiv \{(a,b) \, | \, a, b \in {\mathbb R}\}\] with associated addition and multiplication formulas: \((a,b) + (c,d) = ((a+c)  , (b + d))\), and \((a,b) * (c,d) = ((ac-bd) , (ad+bc))\).

This definition is clear and rigorous, but it has two disadvantages: First, \({\mathbb R}\) is not a subset of this set, but we want \({\mathbb R}\subset {\mathbb C}\). We solve this problem by identifying (refusing to distinguish) \(x \in {\mathbb R}\) with \((x,0) \in {\mathbb C}\). (The alternative is to use \({\mathbb C}= ({\mathbb R}\times {\mathbb R}) - ({\mathbb R}\times \{0\}) \cup {\mathbb R}\) instead, but that forces the sum and product rules to break into cases.)
Next, the definition requires us to write complex numbers in the form “\((2,5)\)”, which is strange and unnatural. We would rather write \(2+5i\). A sleight of hand solves the problem: First, we define \(i\) to be the complex number \((0,1)\). With the identifications \(a = (a,0)\) and \(b=(b,0)\) in mind, we compute \(a+bi=(a,0)+(b,0)(0,1) = (a,b)\), as desired. Thus \(a+bi =(a,b)\) is not a “shorthand” but a legitimate computation.
There is another option for the definition, for those who know a little ring theory:

Definition 2 \({\mathbb C}\) is that quotient ring of \({\mathbb R}[i]\) (here, \(i\) is used as an indeterminant variable, just like the variable usually written \(x\)) obtained by modding out by the principle ideal generated by \(i^2+1\). \[{\mathbb C}= {\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\]

This definition has many advantages: It explains the addition and multiplication formulas, it makes it trivial to see that \({\mathbb C}\) is a ring, and pretty easy to show that \({\mathbb C}\) is a field. But the elements of \({\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\) are cosets, and we really don’t want complex numbers to be cosets, so it adds an unnecessary level of complication. Again we have the problem that \({\mathbb R}\) is not a subset of \({\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\), but it is standard practice in algebra to identify a ring \(R\) with its image in \(R[x]\) or \(R/I\), and these conventions give us \({\mathbb R}\subset {\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\).

Theorem 1 The definitions are equivalent in the sense that both structures are fields and are isomorphic.


Proof. Since \(i^2+1 \in {\mathbb R}[i]\) is monic of degree \(2\), every element of \({\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\) can be written uniquely in the form \(a+bi\) (The linear polynomial remaining after polynomial long division by \(i^2+1\).) We may define \(\phi:{\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1) \to {\mathbb R}\times {\mathbb R}\) by \(\phi(a+bi) = (a,b)\). It’s easy to check that addition and multiplication are preserved. It follows that \({\mathbb R}\times {\mathbb R}\) is a ring (in the first place! We hadn’t yet checked it.) and is isomorphic to \({\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\). To show that \({\mathbb R}[i]/(i^2+1)\) is a field, note that \({\mathbb R}[i]\) is a PID and \(i^2+1\) is irreducible, so \((i^2+1)\) is a maximal ideal. Thus the quotient is a field. 

The fact that it is a field indicates that it is a full number system – no other combinations of \(i\) are necessary. It’s reassuring that quotients \((a+bi)/(c+di)\) exist, but we also need to calculate them. To find the reciprocal of a complex number \(a+bi\), we apply the following trick:
\[\frac{1}{a+bi} = \frac{a-bi}{(a+bi)(a-bi)} = \frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2} = \frac{a}{a^2+b^2} + \frac{-b}{a^2+b^2} i\]
Note that the trick fails exactly when \(a+bi=0\). The number \(a-bi\) is called the conjugate of \(a+bi\). The conjugate function is usually written with an overline: \(\overline{a+bi} = a-bi\).

Exercise 1 (Factoring 13) The Gaussian integers are numbers of the form \(a+bi\) for \(a, b \in {\mathbb Z}\). They form a ring, usually written \({\mathbb Z}[i]\). They play the role of integers for the complex numbers. Prove that the “prime” number \(13\) is the product of two smaller Gaussian integers. Here “smaller” means in norm: \(w\) is smaller than \(z\) if \(|w|<|z|\).


Exercise 2 (Matrix representation) Show that the system of all matrices of the form \(\left(\begin{array}{cc}\alpha & -\beta \\ \beta & \alpha \end{array}\right)\) (with \(\alpha, \beta \in {\mathbb R}\)) with matrix addition and multiplication is isomorphic to the field of complex numbers. Furthermore, show that any such matrix can be written in the form \(\left(\begin{array}{cc}r & 0 \\ 0 & r \end{array}\right)
\cdot\left(\begin{array}{cc}\cos(\theta) & -\sin(\theta) \\ \sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta) \end{array}\right)\) for some \(r\in [0,\infty)\) and \(\theta\in [0, 2\pi)\).

title: Complex Analysis
text:
2.2 More operations
We have four more operations on complex numbers which help us understand them in terms of real numbers:

Definition 3 We define four special functions on \({\mathbb C}\): For a complex number \(z=a+bi\), we define:

\(\overline{z} = a-bi\). This is called the conjugate of \(z\).
\(|z| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\). This is called the modulus of \(z\).
\(\Re(z) = Re(z) = a\). This is called the real part of \(z\).
\(\Im(z) = Im(z) = b\). This is called the imaginary part of \(z\). Notice that the “imaginary part” is a real number!



Proposition 1 For any complex numbers \(w\) and \(z\):

\(|z|^2 = z \overline{z}\)
\(Re(z) = \frac{1}{2}(z+\overline{z})\)
\(Im(z) = \frac{1}{2i}(z-\overline{z})\)
\(|wz| = |w||z|\).



Exercise 3 Prove the above proposition by writing \(z\) in the form \(z=a+bi\). (This technique – proving things by writing \(z\) in the form \(a+bi\) is one we wish to outgrow, and the statement of this proposition will help us do so. We do not wish to constantly regard \(z\) as two variables to be independently manipulated!)

So all four special functions can be expressed using the conjugate. What makes conjugation so special? To start, it’s an automorphism of \({\mathbb C}\):

Exercise 4 (Conjugation is an automorphism) Verify by direct calculation, using the definitions of \(+\) and \(\cdot\), that \(z \mapsto \overline{z}\) is a field homomorphism from \({\mathbb C}\) to \({\mathbb C}\). In order to show that it is bijective, provide its inverse function. Verify that conjugation fixes every element of \({\mathbb R}\).


Corollary 1 For complex numbers \(w\) and \(z\):

\(\overline{w\pm z} = \overline{w}\pm \overline{z}\)
\(\overline{wz} = \overline{w}\) \(\overline{z}\)
\(\overline{w/z} = \overline{w}/\overline{z}\)


Of course the identity map \(id:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\) is also an automorphism fixing \({\mathbb R}\). But there are no other such maps. In the language of Galois Theory, conjugation is the single nontrivial element of the Galois group of \({\mathbb C}\) over \({\mathbb R}\).

Exercise 5 Prove that any field automorphism \(\phi:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\) which fixes \({\mathbb R}\) must be conjugation or the identity. (Hint: What can \(\phi(i)\) be?)

title: Complex Analysis
text:
2.3 Basic Inequalities and relations
Algebra is powerful, but we wish to study the analysis of \({\mathbb C}\). Analysis begins with inequalities.

Theorem 2 For any complex number \(z\): \[-|z| \leq Re(z) \leq |z| \hspace{3em}\text{ and}\hspace{3em} -|z| \leq Im(z) \leq |z|\] …with equality, respectively, if \(z\) is nonpositive real, nonnegative real, nonpositive imaginary (i.e., \(bi\) for \(b \leq 0\)), and nonnegative imaginary.


Exercise 6 Prove the previous proposition by writing \(z=a+bi\) and using properties of real numbers \(a\) and \(b\).

Metric topological reasoning requires a triangle inequality in \({\mathbb C}\):

Proposition 2 (Triangle Inequality) Let \(w\) and \(z\) be complex numbers. Then: 1. \(|w \pm z| \leq  |w|+|z|\) with equality if and only if \(z=0\) or \(w/z \in {\mathbb R}^\pm\)

\(|w \pm z| \geq |w|-|z|\) with equality if and only if \(z=0\) or \(w/z \in {\mathbb R}^\mp\)



Proof. The modulus of a sum \(|w+z|\) involves an inconvenient square root of a sum. It can be avoided by reasoning about square modulus instead:
\(|w+z|^2 = (w+z)\overline{(w+z)} = w\overline{w} + z\overline{z} + w \overline{z}+\overline{w}z = |w|^2 + |z|^2 +
w \overline{z}+\overline{w \overline{z}} = |w|^2 + |z|^2 + 2Re(w\overline{z})\)
Now Proposition 1.7 allows us to relate \(Re(w\overline{z})\) to \(|w\overline{z}| = |w||\overline{z}| = |w||z|\), obtaining:
\(|w|^2 + |z|^2 - 2|w||z|\leq |w+z|^2 \leq |w|^2 + |z|^2 + 2|w||z|\), thus
\((|w|-|z|)^2 \leq |w+z|^2 \leq (|w|+|z|)^2\). All these values except possibly the far left are positive real numbers, so we may drop the squares:
\(|w|-|z| \leq |w+z| \leq |w|+|z|\).
Again by Proposition 1.7, equality holds, respectively, when \(w\overline{z}\) is nonpositive real, or nonnegative real, respectively. If \(z \neq 0\), \(w \overline{z} = |z|^2 w/z\), and \(|z|^2\) is necessarily positive real.
This completes the proof for \(|w+z|\). For the case \(|w-z|\) simply apply the first case with \(-z\) in place of \(z\). 


Exercise 7 Use the triangle inequality to prove that \(|z_1 + z_2 + \ldots + z_n| \leq |z_1| + |z_2| + \ldots + |z_n|\)

title: Complex Analysis
text:
2.4 Polar representation
Let \(w = a+bi\) be a complex number. Let \(r\) denote the distance from \(0\) and \(\theta\) denote the counterclockwise angle from the positive real axis, in radians. Note that we have already discussed an operation on \(w\) that yields \(r\), namely \(r=|w|\). The operation which yields \(\theta\) is called \(\arg(w)\), but it is not well behaved because \(\theta+n2\pi\) has the same geometric significance as \(\theta\). Usually we insist \(\arg(w) \in [0, 2\pi)\)(sometimes \((-\pi, \pi]\)). This makes \(\arg\) a definitive function on \({\mathbb C}- \{0\}\), but doesn’t make it continuous.
Notice that \(a = |w| \cos(\theta)\) and \(b = |w| \sin(\theta)\), so \(w = |w| (\cos(\theta) + i\sin(\theta))\). The parenthesized portion is called \(\operatorname{cis}(\theta)\):

Definition 4 \[\operatorname{cis}(\theta) \equiv_{\text{def}} \cos(\theta) + i \sin(\theta)\]

Thus \(w = |w|\operatorname{cis}(\theta)\).

Proposition 3 The function \(\operatorname{cis}:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb C}\) has the following properties

\(\operatorname{cis}(0)=1\)
\(\operatorname{cis}(\alpha+\beta) = \operatorname{cis}(\alpha)\operatorname{cis}(\beta)\)
\(\operatorname{cis}(\alpha-\beta) = \operatorname{cis}(\alpha) / \operatorname{cis}(\beta)\)
\(\operatorname{cis}(n\alpha) = \operatorname{cis}(\alpha)^n\).
\(|\operatorname{cis}(\theta)| = 1\)



Proof. Parts 1 and 5 are obvious. 2 is essentially the angle sum formulas for \(\cos\) and \(\sin\). (Digression: Proof of angle sum formulas, using geometry: Represent the angle \(\theta+\phi\) as on a unit circle, then drop a perpendicular to the angle \(\theta\), and from there another perpendicular to \(x\)-axis, and calculate the height.) 3 follows from 2. 4 follows from 2 with induction. 

We would like to claim that \(\frac{d}{d\theta} \operatorname{cis}(\theta) = -\sin(\theta) + i\cos(\theta) = i\operatorname{cis}(\theta)\). Compare to normal rules for differentiating exponential functions \(\frac{d}{dt} e^{kt} = ke^{kt}\), which reproduce the same function times a constant. We can’t explain the formula \(\frac{d}{d\theta} \operatorname{cis}(\theta) = i\operatorname{cis}(\theta)\) without a theory of derivatives of functions \(f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb C}\). We are nevertheless tempted by this derivative calculation and by parts 1-4 above to regard \(\operatorname{cis}\) as a kind of exponentiation. Later we will learn that \(\operatorname{cis}(\theta) = e^{i\theta}\), but we are not yet ready to even define complex exponentiation. The students should understand, however, that \(\operatorname{cis}\) is a “temporary” notation, to be replaced later. All of our theorems about \(\operatorname{cis}\) will be regarded, later, as theorems about \(e^{i\theta}\).

Exercise 8 Use the laws for \(\operatorname{cis}(\theta)\) to derive “triple angle formulas” for \(\sin\) and \(\cos\). Do not use the angle sum formulas directly (although of course the proof of proposition Proposition 3 depends on them).


Exercise 9 The function \(\operatorname{cis}\) is a group homomorphism. What are its domain and range? (Tell each group by telling the set and its operation.) What is its kernel?


Exercise 10 Find the sixth roots of unity. Give their values arithmetically and include a picture of them in the complex plane. Together they form a group, by proposition Proposition 3 (do not prove), isomorphic to what familiar group? What is the operation of the group? What is the identity of the group?

title: Complex Analysis
text:
2.5 Geometry of operations
If \({\mathbb C}\) can be identified with \({\mathbb R}\times {\mathbb R}\), then it is the domain of classical Euclidean geometry. Complex operations should have geometric interpretations. What is the geometric significance of addition? of multiplication?
Addition is vector addition, so it corresponds geometrically to the parallelogram rule. Using polar coordinates, we can now derive the geometric significance of multiplication: If \(w = |w| \operatorname{cis}(\alpha)\) and \(z = |z| \operatorname{cis}(\beta)\) are complex numbers, then \(wz = |w||z|\operatorname{cis}(\alpha)\operatorname{cis}(\beta) = |w||z|\operatorname{cis}(\alpha+\beta)\), a complex number whose norm is the product, and whose argument is the sum. In short, magnitudes multiply and angles add. Note that for any fixed \(w \in {\mathbb C}\), the map \(z \mapsto wz\) is a fairly simple transformation of the plane – an expansion by a factor of \(|w|\), and a rotation by \(\arg(w)\), fixing the origin.
We now summarize the geometric significance of each of the fundamental operations on complex numbers:

Addition can be interpreted as a parallelogram rule, as for vectors.
Subtraction can be interpreted as a parallelogram rule with a reversal, as for vectors.
Multiplication requires multiplication of moduli and addition of angles.
Division requires division of moduli and subtraction of angles.
Modulus represents distance from \(0\).
Conjugation is a vertical flip over the real axis.
Real part and imaginary part are horizontal and vertical coordinate.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
2.6 The Riemann Sphere
For real functions, we often attach \(\infty\) and \(-\infty\) to the system \({\mathbb R}\), but not algebraically: \(8+\infty\) is not defined. We do attach them topologically, though: \(\lim_{a \to \infty} f(x)\) and \(\lim_{a \to 0} f(x) = \infty\) are both defined. Topologically speaking, the extended real line is a compactification of \({\mathbb R}\), a topological extension space which is compact.
The extension of \({\mathbb C}\) is similar in that it is topological, and causes these limits to be defined. It is different in the following ways:

There is only one infinity. The alternative was not two, but infinitely many, one for each direction of escape! (This “alternative” comment is open-ended. It could suggest spaces isomorphic to \(P^2_{\mathbb R}\), a closed unit disk, or even the Stone-Cech compactification.)
We often allow a substantial amount of arithmetic with infinity: \(a * \infty = \infty\) (for nonzero \(a\)) , \(a / \infty =0\), and \(a+\infty = a-\infty = \infty\). In fact the only arithmetical forms we don’t allow are \(\infty \pm \infty\), \(\infty / \infty\), \(0 * \infty\), \(0/0\). We even allow \(a/0 = \infty\) and \(b/\infty = 0\). However, we cannot do these things without spoiling the field structure of \({\mathbb C}\), so the extended system is not a good algebraic structure. The guiding principle is whether or not a potential operation \(a \star b\) is continuous near infinity, zero, or wherever, as a function of both of its inputs. To explain this we need to have a topology in place which allows us to define continuity.
We use a sphere model to picture \({\mathbb C}\cup \{\infty\}\), and linear projection to explain the correspondence. Therefore we need to:
define a topological structure on the Riemann sphere and show it topologically equivalent to the sphere. We can do this via standard compactifications. (illustrated b/c you haven’t seen compactifications!)
We use coordinatized analytic geometry to compare the sphere to the Riemann Sphere in a nontrivial way.


2.6.1 The projection
We define a map \(p\) from \(S^2 - \{(0,0,1)\}\) to \({\mathbb C}\) by projection from the north pole, identifying \({\mathbb C}\) with the \(x-y\) plane in \({\mathbb R}^3\) (That is, \(a+bi\) is identified with \((a,b,0) \in {\mathbb R}^3\)). We wish to find a formula for this projection map, in both directions. Let us write \((x_1, x_2, x_3)\) for an arbitrary point on \(S^2\), subject of course to the condition \(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\), and let us write \(z = a+bi\) for an arbitrary point on \({\mathbb C}\), which we identify with the vector \((a,b,0) \in {\mathbb R}^3\). Since \((x_1, x_2, x_3)\) is on the line connecting \((0,0,1)\) to \((a,b,0)\), we have some \(t\) for which \(t(0,0,1) + (1-t)(a,b,0) = (x_1, x_2, x_3)\). We see immediately that \(t=x_3\), so \(a = \frac{x_1}{1-x_3}\) and \(b = \frac{x_2}{1-x_3}\). This gives the formula for \(z = a+bi\) in terms of \((x_1, x_2, x_3)\): \[z = a+bi = p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = \frac{x_1 + i x_2}{1-x_3}\]
We wish to also provide a formula for the inverse function. This is harder because we must solve for \(x_1\), \(x_2\), and \(x_3\) in terms of \(z = a+bi\). We begin by taking square moduli of the equation above. (Note the denominator \(1-x_3\) is a real constant.)
\[\begin{aligned}
|z|^2 &= \frac{x_1^2 + x_2^2}{(1-x_3)^2} \\
&= \frac{1-x_3^2}{(1-x_3)^2} & \text{ (because $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ is on the sphere.)} \\
&= \frac{1+x_3}{1-x_3} & \text{ (cancel after factoring $1-x_3^2$) } \\
\end{aligned}\]
We multiply by \(1-x_3\) to solve for \(x_3\):
\[|z|^2 - |z|^2x_3 = 1+x_3 \hspace{2em} \text{ and } \hspace{2em} x_3 = \frac{|z|^2 - 1}{|z|^2+1}\]
It follows that the denominator \(1-x_3\) is equal to \(1-x_3 = \frac{2}{|z|^2+1}\). Since \(x_1 = a(1-x_3)\) and \(x_2 = b(1-x_3)\) we now have:
\[x_1 = \frac{2a}{\left| z \right|^2+1} \hspace{3em} x_2 = \frac{2b}{\left| z \right|^2+1} \hspace{3em} x_3 = \frac{\left| z \right|^2-1}{\left| z \right|^2+1}\]
\[p^{-1}(z) = \left(\frac{2a}{\left| z \right|^2+1}, \frac{2b}{\left| z \right|^2+1}, \frac{\left| z \right|^2-1}{\left| z \right|^2+1}\right)\]
The maps \(p\) and \(p^{-1}\) above are continuous and give a topological homeomorphism between \({\mathbb C}\) and \(S^2 - \{(0,0,1)\}\). Notice that the algebra above fails if \(1-x_3=0\). There is only one such point on the sphere, namely the north pole itself \((0,0,1)\). Here the geometry of the “unique” line through the north pole and itself also fails, but this is our intention. The coordinate \(x_3\) is an increasing function of \(|z|\), taking values in \([-1,1)\), and that regions \(B(0,M) \subseteq {\mathbb C}\) correspond to regions \(\left \{(x_1,x_2,x_3) \in S^2 | x_3 < \frac{M^2-1}{M^2+1}\right \}\). As \(|z|\) grows larger, \(x_3\) approaches \(1\). The set \({\mathbb C}\cup \{\infty\}\) is not a topological space in any reasonable way, but the completed set \(S^2\) is. By extending \(p\) and \(p^{-1}\) so identify \(p(0,0,1) = \infty\) and \(p^{-1}(\infty) = (0,0,1)\), we can assign a topology to \({\mathbb C}\cup \{\infty\}\) homeomorphic to that of \(S^2\), making \(p\) a homeomorphism by fiat.

Exercise 11 For each of the functions from \({\mathbb C}\) to \({\mathbb C}\), find a formula for the corresponding function from \(S^2\) to \(S^2\) (in \(x_1, x_2, x_3\) coordinates.) You can do this by creating the composition \(p^{-1}\circ f \circ p\) of maps \(S^2 \to {\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\to S^2\) and simplifying algebraically.
For each function, describe how the resulting spherical function can be interpreted as a geometric motion on the sphere.

\(f(z) = \overline{z}\)
\(g(z) = -z\)
\(h(z) = 1/z\)



Exercise 12 (hard) Prove that circles on \(S^2\) correspond, by stereographic projection, to circles and lines on \({\mathbb C}\). Which circles on \(S^2\) correspond to lines on \({\mathbb C}\)? Explain with proof.


Exercise 13 (hard). Let \(w, z \in {\mathbb C}\) and let \(d(w, z)\) denote the distance between the points corresponding to \(w\) and \(z\) on \(S^2\). Prove: \[d(w,z) = \frac{2\left| w-z \right|}{\sqrt{1+\left| w \right|^2}\sqrt{1+\left| z \right|^2}}\]

title: Complex Analysis
text:
3.1 Metric Spaces

Definition 5 A metric space is a set \(X\) together with a function \(d:X \times X \to {\mathbb R}\) (called a distance function or metric) so that

(Zero) \(d(x,y)=0\) iff \(x=y\)
(Nonnegative) \(d(x,y) \geq 0\)
(Symmetry) \(d(x,y) = d(y,z)\)
(Triangle inequality) \(d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z)\)


The two main examples are \({\mathbb R}\) with distance function \(d(x,y) = |y-x|\) (absolute value) and \({\mathbb C}\) with distance function \(d(w,z) = |z-w|\). These two alone justify the abstraction above, but there are countless other important metric spaces. Note that we have proven the triangle inequality for \({\mathbb C}\).
Some discussion: Analysis is often a game of estimation, defined by proving that some absolute difference \(|P-Q|\) is less than \(\varepsilon\). Any proof that \(|P-Q| < \varepsilon\) with arbitrary \(\varepsilon>0\) is a roundabout way to prove the equality \(P=Q\). The role of the triangle inequality is to estimate by waypoints: If \(P\) is nearly \(P'\), which is close to \(Q'\), which is about \(Q\), we find a way to prove \(|P-P'|<\varepsilon/3\), \(|P'-Q'|<\varepsilon/3\), and \(|Q'-Q|<\varepsilon/3\). The combination of these facts to say \(|P-Q|<\varepsilon\) is the triangle inequality. Such a proof is usually written this way: \(|P-Q| = |P-P'+P'-Q'+Q'-Q|  \leq_{\text{(triangle inequality)}}  |P-P'|+|P'-Q'|+|Q'-Q|
< \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = \varepsilon\). Note that the first step seems “magical” until we become accustomed the trick.

Definition 6 An open ball \(B(x,\varepsilon)\) in a metric space \(X\) is a set of the form \(\{y\in X | d(x,y)<\varepsilon\}\). A closed ball is similar: \(\overline{B}(x, \varepsilon) = \{ y \in X | d(x,y)\leq \varepsilon\}\).


Definition 7 A set \(A\) is open if every point \(a \in A\) is contained in some open ball \(a \in B(a,\varepsilon) \subseteq A\). A set is closed if its complement is open.

The terms open and closed are oddly chosen, since a set can be both, or neither. Perhaps whoever chose these terms was unfamiliar with doors.

Proposition 4 The set of open sets in a metric space \((X,d)\) satisfies the axioms for open sets in an abstract topology. That is,

\(\emptyset\) and \(X\) are open sets.
Unions of arbitrary families of open sets are open.
Intersections of finite families of open sets are open.



Proposition 5 The set of closed sets in a metric space \((X,d)\) satisfies the axioms for closed sets in an abstract topology. That is,

\(\emptyset\) and \(X\) are closed sets.
Intersections of arbitrary families of closed sets are closed.
Unions of finite families of closed sets are closed.



Definition 8 (Iota notation) We write the symbol “\(\iota\)” (a Greek iota), pronounced “that” or “the unique,” to refer to some definite thing by means of a property that it alone has. The complete notation treats \(\iota\) as a quantifier: \[ \iota x \enspace P(x) \] and means the unique value of \(x\) such that \(P(x)\). If no such value or multiple values exist, we interpret \(\iota x\) as an error and say that $ x P(x) $ does not exist.

For example, “\(\iota x \enspace x^3 = 64\)” means “the unique \(x\) whose cube is \(64\),” which of course is \(4\): \((\iota x \enspace x^3 = 64) = 4\). On the contrary, “\(\iota x \enspace x > 0\)” fails to refer to anything. This should remind the reader of standard limit notation, which can also fail to refer to any answer if a limit “is not defined” or “does not exist”. In fact, limits can be described as a special case of \(\iota\)-notation, and we will often define limits below using \(\iota\).
The notation “\(\iota\)” is Bertrand Russell’s notation for definite description, but our policy for interpretation differs from Russell’s. The symbol \(\iota x\) acts like a quantifier in that it anticipates a statement involving \(x\), but a statement \(\iota x  P(x)\) is grammatically a noun clause, not a complete statement.

Definition 9 (Sequence convergence) Let \((x_n)_{n \in {\mathbb N}}\) be a sequence in a metric space \(X\). The limit of the sequence is defined to be \[\lim_{n\to \infty} x_n \equiv \iota L \enspace \forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists N \enspace \forall n > N \enspace |x_n - L|< \varepsilon\] equivalently, \[\lim_{n\to \infty} x_n \equiv \iota L \enspace\forall \text{ open } U \ni L \enspace \exists N \enspace \forall n>N \enspace x_n \in U\]

Of course the limit of a sequence may or may not exist. If it exists we say that \(x_n\) is convergent and that it converges to \(L\). We write \(x_n \to L\). (If a limit is bad, like \(\lim_{n \to \infty} (-1)^n\), we contend that it lacks existence, not definition. Any sequential limit in a metric space is “defined” in the literal sense that a definition is provided above and an alternate definition would conflict. This author’s position – that a notation can be “defined” but not refer to an existent thing – is not standard.)

Exercise 14 Prove the implied equivalence in the previous definition


Proposition 6 (Sequentially closed and open) Let \(X\) be a metric space. A set \(A \subseteq X\) is closed if and only if for any convergent sequence \((x_n) \subseteq A\), the limit \(\lim_n x_n \in A\). On the other hand, a set \(A\) is open if and only if no sequence outside \(A\) converges to a point of \(A\).*

The reader should beware that in nonmetric topologies, convergence of sequences does not characterize open and closed sets.

Definition 10 Let \(A \subseteq X\) be a subset of a metric space. The interior of \(A\), written \(A^0\) is, equivalently,

\(\bigcup \{U\,|\,U \subseteq A, U \text{ open}\}\)
\(\{x \in X \,|\, x \in U \subseteq A \text{ for some open $U$}\}\)
\(\{x \in X \,|\, B(x,\varepsilon) \subseteq A \text{ for some $\varepsilon>0$}\}\)



Exercise 15 Prove the implied equivalences in the previous definition


Definition 11 Let \(A \subseteq X\) be a subset of a metric space. The closure of \(A\), written \(\overline{A}\) is, equivalently,

\(\bigcap \{C\,|\,C \supseteq A, C \text{ closed}\}\)
\(\{x \in X \,|\, U \cap A \neq \emptyset  \text{ for every open $U \ni x$}\}\)
\(\{x \in X \,|\, B(x,\varepsilon) \cap A \neq \emptyset \text{ for every $\varepsilon>0$}\}\)
\(\{x \in X \,|\, x \text{ is the limit of some sequence $(x_n)$ in $A$}\}\)



Exercise 16 Prove the implied equivalences in the previous definition

In general \(A^0 \subseteq A \subseteq \overline{A}\). Any open set equals its interior, and any closed set equals its closure.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
3.2 Continuity

Definition 12 A function \(f: (X,d) \to (Y,\rho)\) from one metric space to another is continuous if, equivalently,

\(\forall x_0 \in X \enspace \forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists \delta>0 \enspace \forall x\in X \enspace d(x,x_0)<\delta \to \rho(f(x),f(x_0)) < \varepsilon\)
For any open set \(U \subseteq Y\), \(f^{-1}(U)\) is open.
For any closed set \(C \subseteq Y\), \(f^{-1}(C)\) is closed.
For any convergent sequence \((x_n)\), \(\lim_n f(x_n) = f(\lim_n x_n)\)



Exercise 17 Prove the implied equivalences in the previous definition

Sequential limits are identified by some integer input (the index) which goes to infinity. A sequence is just a function of such an input. We also have limits in which some input \(x\), varying in a metric space \(X\), approaches a fixed point \(x_0\). Thus we define the limit of a (not necessarily continuous!) function defined on \(X\).

Definition 13 Let \(f: (X,d) \to (Y,\rho)\) be a function from a metric space to another. Let \(x_0 \in X\). We define the limit: \[\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) \equiv_{def} \iota y_0 \in Y \enspace \forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists \delta >0 \enspace \forall x \in X \enspace 0<d(x,x_0)<\delta \to \rho(f(x),y_0)<\varepsilon\]

As in basic Calculus, the limit \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)\) may or may not exist. Note that this empowers us to discuss \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)\) when \(f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}\), \(f:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\), \(f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb C}\), or \(f:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb R}\). All four cases will be important.

Definition 14 A function \(f\) is continuous at \(x_0\) if \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = f(x_0)\).

Note that continuity at \(x_0\) does not require continuity, not even in a neighborhood of \(x_0\). But if \(f\) is continuous at every point, it is continuous.
If we have a sequence \(\{f_n\}\) of functions and a sequence \((x_m)\) of inputs, we may take limits in two ways: \(\lim_{n \to \infty} \lim_{m \to \infty} f_n(x_m)\) and \(\lim_{m \to \infty} \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_m)\). Limits of this type do not always commute, and we must use caution to distinguish them carefully.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
3.3 Connectedness

Definition 15 A set \(U\) in a metric space \((X,d)\) is clopen if it is both open and closed.


Definition 16 A metric space \(X\) is disconnected if it is the union of two nonempty disjoint open sets. Equivalently, if it has a clopen set other than \(\emptyset\) and \(X\). A subset \(A \subset X\) is disconnected if the metric space \((A,d)\) is disconnected. A set is connected if it is not disconnected.


Proposition 7 Intervals in \({\mathbb R}\) (i.e., sets of the form \((a,b)\), \([a,b]\), \([a,b)\), or \((a,b]\), where \(a\) might be \(-\infty\) and \(b\) might be \(+\infty\)) are connected, and every connected set is an interval.


Proposition 8 Let \(f:X \to Y\) be a continuous map of metric spaces, with \(X\) connected. Then \(f(X)\) is connected.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
3.4 Compactness

Definition 17 A topological space \(A\) is called compact if, equivalently,

Every open cover \(A = \bigcup_{\alpha \in I} U_\alpha\) has a finite subcover \(A = \bigcup_{i=1}^n U_{\alpha_i}\).
Every family \(\mathcal F\) of closed subsets of \(A\) with the finite intersection property (i.e., any finite subfamily has nonempty intersection) has nonempty intersection (i.e., \(\bigcap \mathcal F \neq \emptyset\)).

If \(A \subset X\) is a subset of a larger topological space \(X\), we call \(A\) compact if it is compact in the subspace topology.


Exercise 18 Prove the implied equivalence in the previous definition

This equivalence is easier than it looks, little more than DeMorgan’s laws.

Theorem 3 Let \(K \subseteq X\) be compact in a metric space \(X\). Then \(K\) is closed.


Proof. If \(x \notin K\), then \(K\) has an open cover of the form \(\{X - \overline{B(x,\varepsilon)} | \varepsilon>0\}\). Any finite subcover of that yields a ball \(B(x,\varepsilon)\) disjoint from \(K\).


Proposition 9 If \(C \subseteq K \subseteq X\), with \(C\) closed and \(K\) compact, then \(C\) is compact.


Proposition 10 Let \(f:X \to Y\) be a continuous function, and \(K \subseteq X\) compact. Then \(f(K)\) is compact.


Proposition 11 The product \(X \times Y\) (in the product topology) of two compact spaces \(X\) and \(Y\) is compact.


Theorem 4 (Heine-Borel Theorem, 1D) Let \(K \subseteq {\mathbb R}\). Then \(K\) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.


Proof. Let \(K\) be compact. Then it is closed, by Theorem 3. Boundedness is trivial. Conversely, it suffices to show that \([a,b]\) is compact, since \(K\) is a closed subset of some closed interval. Let \([a,b] \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal U\), where \(\mathcal U\) is a family of open sets. We use a connectedness argument. Let \[C = \{c \in [a,b] \,|\, [a,c]\text{ can be covered by a finite subcollection of } {\mathcal U}\}\] If \([a,c]\) is finitely covered, then we have \(c \in B(c,\varepsilon) \subseteq U_c \in \mathcal U\), and for any \(c' \in B(c,\varepsilon)\), \([a,c']\) is finitely covered by the same cover. So \(C\) is open. On the other hand, if \([a,c]\) is not finitely covered, then \(c \in B(c,\varepsilon) \subseteq U_c \in \mathcal U\). If any \(c' \in B(c,\varepsilon)\) were such that \([a,c']\) were finitely coverable, then \([a,c]\) could be finitely covered by adding the cover element \(U_c\). So \([a,b] - C\) is also open. Since \(a \in C\), connectedness yields \([a,b] = C\) as desired. 


Theorem 5 (Heine-Borel Theorem) Let \(K \subseteq {\mathbb R}^n\). Then \(K\) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.


Proof. If \(K\) is closed and bounded, it’s a subset of some interval product \([a_1, b_1] \times
\ldots \times [a_n, b_n]\), which is compact by the previous two statements. 

Caution: For many students, “closed and bounded” is conceptually easier than “compact” and the Heine-Borel theorem sounds like permission not to grapple with the subtleties of open covers. Please note that “compact” is a question of general topology, but “bounded” is meaningless in nonmetric spaces. Moreover, simple metric spaces other than \({\mathbb R}^n\) often have closed bounded noncompact sets. The Heine-Borel property is a specialized result for a specialized space and shouldn’t underpin one’s concept of compactness!

title: Complex Analysis
text:
3.5 Completeness
Consider the sequence \(x_n = 1/n\) in the space \({\mathbb R}\) and also in the space \({\mathbb R}- \{0\}\). In the former, it converges to zero, but in the latter it is a divergent sequence. In \({\mathbb R}- \{0\}\), there is no way to measure how close \(x_n\) gets to \(0\), but we can say that the sequence terms get close to one another. The Cauchy criterion expresses that the terms of a sequence get close to each other. Of course it is strongly related to convergence. (In fact, Cauchy called this condition “convergence”!)

Definition 18 Let \(x_n\) be a sequence in a metric space. We call \(x_n\) Cauchy if \[\forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists N \enspace \forall m>N \enspace \forall n>N \enspace d(x_m, x_n) < \varepsilon\]

Note that the definition of convergence depends on the limit point, which may not be known, whereas the Cauchy condition depends only on the terms of the sequence.

Proposition 12 Every convergent sequence is Cauchy.


Exercise 19 Prove the previous proposition.

Returning to the sequence \(x_n = 1/n\), we see that it converges in \({\mathbb R}\), so it is Cauchy. Despite being Cauchy, it does not converge in \({\mathbb R}- \{0\}\), and this can be considered a “flaw” with the metric space \({\mathbb R}- \{0\}\). Spaces without such problems are called complete:

Definition 19 Let \(X\) be a metric spaces. We call \(X\) complete if every Cauchy sequence in \(X\) converges.


Proposition 13 \({\mathbb R}\) is complete.


Proof. Let \(x_n\) be a Cauchy sequence in \({\mathbb R}\). Since \(x_n\) is Cauchy, it is bounded in some interval \([a,b]\). For each \(N\), let \(C_N\) be the closure of the tail sequence \(\{x_N, x_{N+1}, \ldots\}\) in \({\mathbb R}\). The sequence \((C_N)\) is a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed sets in a compact set, so there is some \(L \in \bigcap C_N\). Now for any \(\varepsilon>0\) we may choose \(N\) so that for all larger \(n,m\) we have \(|x_m-x_n| < \varepsilon/2\). But the tail sequence \(\{x_N, x_{N+1}, \ldots\}\) has within it some \(x_n\in B(L, \varepsilon/2)\). By the triangle inequality, \(\{x_N, x_{N+1}, \ldots\} \subseteq B(L, \varepsilon)\). 


Corollary 2 \({\mathbb R}^n\) and \({\mathbb C}\) are complete.


Proof. A Cauchy sequence \((v_n)\) in \({\mathbb R}^n\) has as its coordinates \(n\) Cauchy sequences on \({\mathbb R}\). They converge individually, producing a vector to which \((v_n)\) converges. 


Exercise 20 Prove that a closed subset of a complete metric space is complete.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
3.6 Uniform convergence and continuity
A sequence of functions \(f_n\) on a space \(X\) produces, for each point \(x \in X\), a sequence \(f_n(x)\). Pointwise convergence refers to the individual convergence of such sequences:

Definition 20 Let \(f_n:X \to Y\) be a sequence of functions. We say \(f_n\) converges pointwise to \(f\) if, for each point \(x \in X\), \(\lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)\). That is,
\[\forall x \in X \enspace \forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists N \enspace \forall n>N \enspace \rho(f(x), f_n(x))< \varepsilon\]

Now if each function \(f_n\) is continuous, it’s natural to expect that the limit function \(f\) is also continuous, but this need not be the case:

Example 1 Let \(f_n:[0,1] \to {\mathbb R}\) by \(f_n(x) = x^n\). Then the sequence of functions converges pointwise to the (discontinuous) function \(f:[0,1] \to {\mathbb R}\) which is identically zero except \(f(1)=1\).

There is a stronger form of convergence, however, which makes things work out better:

Definition 21 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of functions. We say that \((f_n)\) converges uniformly to \(f\) if \[\forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists N \enspace \forall n>N \enspace \forall x \in X \enspace \rho(f(x), f_n(x))< \varepsilon\]

The only difference between this definition and the previous is the relative ordering of “\(\forall x \in X\)” and “\(\exists N\)”. Thus the difference between pointwise convergence and uniform convergence is that uniform convergence allows us to choose \(N\), depending on \(\varepsilon>0\), but not depending on \(x\). Abstractly, “\(\exists N \forall x \, P(N,x)\)” implies “\(\forall x \exists N \, P(N,x)\)”, so uniform convergence implies convergence. The example above, restricted to the interval \([0,1/2]\) converges uniformly because \(|f_n(x)| \leq 2^{-n}\). The point of this refined notion of convergence is that the uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous:

Theorem 6 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of continuous functions converging uniformly to \(f\). Then \(f\) is continuous.


Proof. In spirit, continuity boils down to the estimation \(f(x) \approx f(x_0)\). Our strategy is to estimate \(f(x) \approx f_n(x) \approx f_n(x_0) \approx f(x_0)\). Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By uniform convergence, choose \(N\) so that \[\forall n>N \enspace \forall x \in X \enspace \rho(f(x), f_n(x))< \varepsilon/3\] Fix some \(n>N\). Let \(x_0\) be fixed. By the continuity assumption on \(f_n\), choose \(\delta>0\) so that \[\text{for given } x_0 \in X \enspace \forall x \in X \enspace \text{ if }d(x_0, x)< \delta \text{ then } \rho(f_n(x), f_n(x_0)) < \varepsilon/3\] Now for given \(x_0 \in X\) and for any \(x \in X\) we have by the triangle inequality for \(\rho\): \[\text{ if }d(x_0, x)< \delta \text{ then }  \rho(f(x),f(x_0)) \leq \rho(f(x),f_n(x))+\rho(f_n(x),f_n(x_0))+ \rho(f_n(x_0),f(x_0)) = \frac{\varepsilon}{3} +\frac{\varepsilon}{3}+\frac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon\] as desired. 

While we’re interchanging quantifiers, we would like to point out a stronger form of continuity in which we convert \(\forall x_0 \enspace \exists \delta\) to \(\exists \delta \enspace \forall x_0\):

Definition 22 Let \(f:X \to Y\). We say that \(f\) is uniformly continuous if \[\forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists \delta>0 \enspace \forall x_0 \in X \enspace \forall x\in X \enspace d(x,x_0)<\delta \to \rho(f(x),f(x_0)) < \varepsilon\]

Given the terminology, the following theorem is obligatory:

Theorem 7 Let \((f_n)\) be a sequence of uniformly continuous functions converging uniformly to \(f\). Then \(f\) is uniformly continuous.


Proof. In the proof of theorem Theorem 6, strike out “Let \(x_0\) be fixed” and replace “given \(x_0\)” with “any \(x_0\)”.


Theorem 8 If \(f:X \to Y\) is continuous on a compact domain \(X\), then \(f\) is uniformly continuous.


Proof. Let \(\varepsilon>0\). For each \(z \in X\), using continuity, choose \(B(z, \delta_z)\) so that for any \(y \in B(z, 2\delta_z)\) we have \(\rho(f(y),f(z))<\varepsilon/2\). Find a finite subcover of the open cover \(\{B(z, \delta_z)\}\), and let \(\delta_0\) be the minimum of all \(\delta_z\) in the subcover. Now let \(x, y \in X\) be arbitrary with \(d(y,x)<\delta_0\). There is some \(z\) (from the finite subcover) with \(d(y,z) \leq \delta_z\), so also \(d(x,z) \leq \delta_0 + \delta_z \leq 2 \delta_z\) so \(\rho(f(y),f(x)) \leq \rho(f(y),f(z))+ \rho(f(z),f(x)) \leq \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon\) as desired. 


Exercise 21 By example, prove that a sequence of uniformly continuous functions on a compact domain can converge, not uniformly, to a uniformly continuous function.

Next we introduce absolute convergence:

Definition 23 We call the series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\) of complex numbers absolutely convergent if the series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty |a_n|\) converges.

Here “absolute” refers to the absolute value function, but in \({\mathbb C}\) the function \(|a_n|\) is usually called modulus. Of course absolute convergence implies convergence. It’s possible to deduce this from the M-test using constant functions \(f_n(z) = a_n\), but a straightforward proof is more informative:

Proof. For \(\varepsilon>0\) choose \(N\) so that for all \(n>m>N\) we have \(\sum_{k=m+1}^n |a_k|< \varepsilon\). This is possible because \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty |a_n|\) converges, so its partial sum sequence is Cauchy. Then by the triangle inequality, \(\left|\sum_{k=m+1}^n a_k\right| < \varepsilon\). This shows that the sequence of partial sums \(\left(\sum_{k=0}^N a_k \right)_{N \in {\mathbb N}}\) is Cauchy, so converges. 

The proof of the M-test uses an infinitary triangle inequality, so we start with that:

Proposition 14 Let \((z_n)\) be a sequence of complex numbers. Then \[\left|\sum_{n=1}^\infty z_n \right| \leq \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left|z_n\right|\]


Proof. \[\left|\sum_{n=1}^\infty z_n\right| = \left|\lim_N \sum_{n=1}^N z_n\right| =\lim_N \left|\sum_{n=1}^N z_n\right| \leq \lim_N \sum_{n=1}^N \left|z_n\right|  = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left|z_n\right|\] …because \(|-|\) is continuous and \(a_n \leq b_n \to \lim a_n \leq \lim b_n\). 

The next theorem is fundamental to our use of power series.

Theorem 9 (Weierstrass M-test) Let \(u_n: X \to {\mathbb C}\) be a sequence of functions having \(\forall x\in X \enspace |u_n(x)| \leq M_n\) for a sequence of bounds \(M_n\). If \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty M_n <\infty\), then \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty u_n\) converges uniformly and absolutely on \(X\).


Proof. First, fix \(x\). Absolute convergence of \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty u_n(x)\) follows from the comparison test since \(|u_n(x)| \leq M_n\). This shows that \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty u_n(x)\) converges pointwise to a function we call \(f(x)\).
For uniform convergence, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) so that \(\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty M_n < \varepsilon\) and let \(n>N\). Then for any \(x\) we have \[\left|f(x) - \sum_{i=1}^n u_i(x)\right| =  \left|\sum_{i=n+1}^\infty u_i(x)\right| \leq \sum_{i=n+1}^\infty \left|u_i(x)\right| \leq \sum_{i=n+1}^\infty M_i < \varepsilon\] as desired. 


Exercise 22 Let \(f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n\) be a power series whose (complex) coefficients \(a_n\) are bounded above in the sense that \(|a_n| \leq B \in {\mathbb R}\) for some \(B\). Prove that the sum \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n z^n\) is uniformly convergent on any disk \(B(0, r)\) with \(0<r<1\).

title: Complex Analysis
text:
4.1 Derivatives and Limits
We define the derivative of a complex-valued function exactly as one would expect:

Definition 24 Let \(f: {\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\). The derivative of \(f\) is defined to be: \[f'(z_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z_0+h)-f(z_0)}{h}\] Equivalently (with \(z = z_0+h\)): \[f'(z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0} \frac{f(z)-f(z_0)}{z-z_0}\] When the derivative exists, we say that \(f\) is differentiable at \(z_0\).

If we unpack this definition we have:
\[f'(z_0)=\iota L \in {\mathbb C}\enspace \forall \varepsilon>0 \enspace \exists \delta >0 \enspace \forall z \in {\mathbb C}\enspace 0<|z-z_0|<\delta \to \left|\frac{f(z)-f(z_0)}{z-z_0} -L\right|<\varepsilon\]
The key difference here is “\(\forall z \in {\mathbb C}\)” instead of “\(\forall z \in {\mathbb R}\)” (which, given the implication, amounts to \(\forall z \in B(z_0, \delta)\) instead of \(\forall z \in (z_0-\delta, z_0+\delta)\)). This is a much larger, two-dimensional set of \(z\) values which must satisfy the condition \(\left|\frac{f(z)-f(z_0)}{z-z_0}-L\right|<\varepsilon\). We will see, thanks to this small change, that differentiability is a much stronger condition on complex functions than it is on real functions. For example, if \(f\) is differentiable, then its derivative \(f'\) is likewise differentiable, and so on.
For now, we distinguish between three conditions later proven equivalent:

Definition 25 Let \(U \subseteq {\mathbb C}\) be an open set. We say that \(f: U \to {\mathbb C}\) is differentiable if \(f'(z)\) exists for all \(z \in U\). We say that \(f\) is continuously differentiable if \(f\) is differentiable and \(f'\) is a continuous function. We say that \(f\) is infinitely differentiable if all higher derivatives \(f^{(n)}(z)\) exist.

Much later, we will prove that these conditions are all equivalent, and replace these terms with the single term analytic. For now we use the more direct language.
We begin with an easy example from which we will later generate more.

Theorem 10 If \(f(z) = mz+b\) (where \(m\), \(b\) are complex constants) then \(f'(z) = m\)


Proof. The expression \(\frac{f(z)-f(z_0)}{z-z_0}\) is always \(m\), independent of both \(z\) and \(z_0\), so the limit exists and equals \(m\).

Before we can prove the various derivative rules, we need some limit laws:

Theorem 11 (Limit Rules) Let \(X\) be a metric space and let \(f, g : X \to {\mathbb C}\) or \({\mathbb C}^n\). (Note this includes the case \(f,g:X \to {\mathbb R}\).) The following equations are true provided their right hand sides exist.

\(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) \pm g(x) = \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) \pm \lim_{x \to x_0} g(x)\)
\(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)g(x) = \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) \cdot \lim_{x \to x_0} g(x)\)
\(\displaystyle \lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)/g(x) = \frac{\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to x_0} g(x)}\)
If \(\square:{\mathbb C}^2 \to {\mathbb C}\) is a continuous binary operation then \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f_1(x) \square f_2(x) = \lim_{x \to x_0} f_1(x) \square \lim_{x \to x_0} f_2(x)\)
If \(\lim_{x \to x_0} g(x) = y_0\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(y_0\), then \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(g(x)) = f(y_0)\)



Proof. First we prove 5. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Choose \(\rho>0\) so that \(|y - y_0|<\rho \to |f(y)-f(y_0)|< \varepsilon\). Choose \(\delta>0\) so that \(0<|x-x_0|<\delta \to |g(x)-y_0|<\rho\). We may substitute \(y=g(x)\) and chain together the implications: \(0<|x-x_0|<\delta \to |f(g(x))-f(y_0)|< \varepsilon\) as desired.
Applying 5 with \(g(x) = (f_1, f_2)\) and \(f=\square\) yields 4. It remains to prove the continuity of arithmetical operations. In each case we assume \(a \square b = c\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), and give a neighborhood \(U = B(a, \delta_1) \times B(b,\delta_2) \subseteq {\mathbb C}\times {\mathbb C}\) so that \(\square(U) \subseteq B(c, \varepsilon)\). For addition and subtraction we may take \(B(a, \varepsilon/2) \times B(b,\varepsilon/2)\), by the triangle inequality. For multiplication suppose hypothetically \(\delta_1>0\) and \(\delta_2>0\) are already chosen. If \((x,y) \in B(a, \delta_1) \times B(b,\delta_2)\) then \(\left| xy-ab \right| \leq \left| xy-bx+bx-ab \right| \leq \left| x \right|\left| y-b \right| + \left| b \right|\left| x-a \right|
< \left| x \right|\delta_2 + \left| b \right|\delta_1 \leq \left| x-a+a \right|\delta_2 + \left| b \right|\delta_1
\leq \delta_1\delta_2 + \left| a \right|\delta_2 + \left| b \right|\delta_1\). We use this computation to guide our choices of \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\). We may make \(\left| b \right|\delta_1 \leq {\varepsilon}/3\) by choosing \(\delta_1 = \frac{{\varepsilon}}{3\left| b \right|}\) (or \(1\) if \(b=0\)). We may then assure that the other two terms are each less than or equal to \({\varepsilon}/3\) by choosing \(\delta_2 = \min(\frac{{\varepsilon}}{3\delta_1},\frac{{\varepsilon}}{3\left| a \right|})\). (Or simply \(\delta_2 = \frac{{\varepsilon}}{3\delta_1}\) if \(a=0\).)
We can deduce the division law from the multiplication law if we can show that \(r(x) = 1/x\) is a continuous function at any \(x_0 \neq 0\). Let \({\varepsilon}>0\) and suppose \(\delta\) somehow already chosen, with \(\left| x-x_0 \right|<\delta\). Then \[\left| \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{x_0} \right| = \left| \frac{x_0-x}{xx_0} \right| < \left| \frac{\delta}{(x-x_0 + x_0)x_0} \right| = {\frac{\delta}{\left| x-x_0 + x_0 \right|\left| x_0 \right|}} \leq {\frac{\delta}{\left| \left| x_0 \right|-\delta \right|\left| x_0 \right|}} =\frac{\delta}{(\left| x_0 \right|-\delta)\left| x_0 \right|}\] provided \(\left| x_0 \right|-\delta\) is positive. If \(\delta < \frac{\left| x_0 \right|}{2}\) it is, and we may furthermore continue \[\leq \frac{\delta}{\frac{\left| x_0 \right|}{2} \left| x_0 \right|} = \frac{2\delta}{|x_0|^2} \leq^? \varepsilon\] Therefore if \(\delta = \min(\frac{x_0}{2}, \frac{{\varepsilon}|x_0|^2}{2})\) we have our result. 


Exercise 23 Let \(f\) be a function and let \(g\) be a continuous function. Consider the limits \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(g(x))\) and \(\lim_{y \to g(x_0)} f(y)\). Does either limit’s existence imply the other’s? Explain with proof. If they both exist are they necessarily equal? Explain with proof.



Exercise 24 Assess whether each function is differentiable. Answer with proof.

\(f(z) = \overline{z}\), at any point \(z\in {\mathbb C}\).
\(f(z) = \left| z \right|^2\), at any point \(z \in {\mathbb C}\). (Hint: Consider \(z=0\) and \(z \neq 0\) as separate cases.)
\(f(z) = \frac{1}{z}\).


We may now begin the theory of differentiable functions in earnest.

Proposition 15 If \(f\) is differentiable, then \(f\) is continuous.


Proof. \[\lim_{w \to z} f(w)-f(z) = \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z} \cdot (w-z) = f'(z)\lim_{w \to z}(w-z) = 0\] 


Theorem 12 (Linear Approximation) Let \(f\) be a complex function defined in a neighborhood of a point \(z\). Then \(f\) is differentiable at \(z\) if and only if there is a linear function \(L\) and an “error” function \(g\) with \(f = L+g\), \(g(z) = 0\), and \(\lim_{w\to z}\frac{g(w)}{w-z}  = 0\).


Proof. A function \(f\) is differentiable at \(z\) exactly when there is a value \(m\) so that \(\lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z} - m=0\) Equivalently \(\lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w) - f(z)- m(w-z)}{w-z} =0\). Notice that \(L(w) = f(z)+m(w-z)\) is linear and the numerator suffices for \(g(w)\). Conversely if \(f=L+g\) as above, then \(f'(z) = L'(z)+g'(z) = m + 0 = m\), so \(f'(z)\) exists. 


Exercise 25 Compare the following two statements about limits: \[\begin{align}
    \lim_{w \to z} g(w)  =& 0 \enspace \text{ versus}\\
    \lim_{w \to z} \frac{g(w)}{w-z}  =& 0        
\end{align}\] One of these statements is logically stronger, meaning that it implies the other. Let us call the stronger statement “S” and the weaker “W”.

Which is which?
Prove \(S \to W\).
Illustrate \(\neg (W \to S)\) by counterexample (and prove it’s a counterexample).
Let \(f\) be a complex function defined in a neighborhood of a point \(z\). Now \(f\) is differentiable at \(z\) if and only if there is a linear function \(L\) and an “error” function \(g\) with \(f = L+g\) and [S] and \(g(z) = 0\). What familiar condition on \(f\) is equivalent to the above, if we replace \(S\) with \(W\)? Answer without proof.



Theorem 13 (Derivative Rules) Let \(f,g:U \to {\mathbb C}\). The following equations are true provided the right hand sides exist:

(sum/difference rule) \(\frac{d}{dz}(f(z) \pm g(z)) = f'(z)\pm g'(z)\)
(constant multiple rule) \(\frac{d}{dz}(kf(z)) = kf'(z)\)
(product rule) \(\frac{d}{dz}(f(z) \cdot g(z)) = f'(z) g(z) + f(z) g'(z)\)
(quotient rule) \(\frac{d}{dz}(f(z)/g(z)) = \frac{f'(z)g(z)-f(z)g'(z)}{(g(z))^2}\)
(chain rule) \(\frac{d}{dz}(f(g(z))) = f'(g(z))g'(z)\)



Proof. The proofs are the same as for real functions \(f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}\), but since students may not have seen proof-based calculus, we provide them.

\(\frac{d}{dz}(f(z) + g(z)) =
        \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w) + g(w) - f(z)-g(z)}{w-z} =
        \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w) - f(z)}{w-z} + \lim_{w \to z} \frac{g(w) - g(z)}{w-z} = f'(z)+g'(z)\)
Exercise (below).
\[\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dz}(f(z)g(z)) &= \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w)g(w)-f(z)g(z)}{w-z} \\
    &= \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w)g(w)-f(z)g(w)+f(z)g(w)-f(z)g(z)}{w-z}\\
    &= \left(\lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z} g(w)\right) + \left(\lim_{x \to z}f(z)\frac{g(w)-g(z)}{w-z}\right)\\
    &= f'(z)g(z) + f(z)g'(z)
\end{align}\]
Exercise (below).
The most attractive demonstration of the chain rule is sadly wrong. It goes like this: \[\begin{align}
    \frac{d}{dz}(f(g(z))) &= \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(g(w))-f(g(z))}{w-z} \\
    &= \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(g(w))-f(g(z))}{g(w)-g(z)} \cdot \lim_{w \to z}\frac{g(w)-g(z)}{w-z} \text{ but see below}\\
    &= f'(g(z)) \cdot g'(z)        
\end{align}\] The problem is that the introduced denominator \(g(w)-g(z)\) may be zero, even though \(w-z\) is not. We therefore replace the fraction \(\frac{f(g(w))-f(g(z))}{g(w)-g(z)}\) with a piecewise defined function designed to deal with that possibility: \[\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dz}(f(g(z))) &= \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(g(w))-f(g(z))}{w-z} \label{eqn:Chain1}\\
&= \lim_{w \to z} \left[\left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{f(g(w))-f(g(z))}{g(w)-g(z)}  & \text{ if $g(w) \neq g(z)$} \\
f'(g(z))& \text{ if $g(w) = g(z)$} \end{array} \right\} \cdot \frac{g(w)-g(z)}{w-z}\right] \label{eqn:Chain2}\\
&= f'(g(z)) \cdot g'(z)
\end{align}\]

Notice that the equality holds true when \(g(w)=g(z)\), because both sides are zero. To evaluate the limit we used the product law and a continuity argument: The piecewise part may be regarded as the composition of \(w \mapsto g(w)\) (continuous at \(w=z\)) with the function \(x \mapsto  \left\{
    \begin{array}{ll}
    \frac{f(x)-f(g(z))}{x-g(z)}  & \text{ if $x \neq g(z)$} \\
    f'(g(z)) & \text{ if $x = g(z)$}
    \end{array}
     \right.\), which is continuous at \(x=g(z)\) by the definition of the derivative \(f'(g(z))\).


Exercise 26 The chain rule makes implicit use of the important function \(q(w,z)\), which we will revisit in section 3.4.
\[q(w,z) = \left\{
    \begin{array}{ll}
        \frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z} & \text{ if } w \neq z \\
        f'(z) & \text{ if } w=z
    \end{array} \right\}
\] However, in the chain rule prove we have the substitution \(q(w,g(z)).\)
Prove:

The function \(q\) is symmetric: \(q(w,z) = q(z,w)\).
If \(f(z)\) is differentiable on \(U \subseteq C\), then \(q(w,z)\) is a continuous function of \(w\) for each fixed \(z \in U\) and vice versa.



Exercise 27 Prove parts 2 and 4 of the previous theorem. For the quotient rule, use common denominator and take inspiration from the product rule.


Exercise 28 Prove that the derivative of \(z^n\) is \(nz^{n-1}\) for all integers \(n \geq 1\). (Hint: Induct on the product rule.) Then prove the same law for integers \(n \leq -1\). Is the law correct for \(n=0\)?

Our last derivative rule is for inverse functions:

Theorem 14 Let \(g(f(z))=z\) for all \(z \in G\) (open), \(f\) continuous at \(z\). Then \[f'(z) = \frac{1}{g'(f(z))}\] provided the right hand side exists.


Proof. The chain rule suffices if we assume \(f'(z)\) exists, but we wish to prove it exists. Instead we directly manipulate the limit using an \(\epsilon-\delta\) argument.
\[\begin{align}
f'(z) &= \lim_{w \to z} \frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z} \\
&= 1 / \lim_{w \to z} \frac{w-z}{f(w)-f(z)} \text{ (provided that limit exists and is nonzero)}\\
&= 1 / \lim_{w \to z} \frac{g(f(w))-g(f(z))}{f(w)-f(z)} \\
\end{align}\]
By assumption, the limit \(g'(f(z)) = \lim_{v \to f(z)} \frac{g(v)-g(f(z))}{v-f(z)}\) exists and equals, say, \(L \neq 0\). If \(\epsilon > 0\), we may choose \(\delta>0\) so that whenever \(0<|v-f(z)|<\delta\) then \(|\frac{g(v)-g(f(z))}{v-f(z)} - L| < \epsilon\). Since \(f\) is continuous, we may furthermore choose \(\rho>0\) so that if \(|w -z|<\rho\) then \(|f(w)-f(z)|<\delta\). But \(f\) is also locally injective, so we may furthermore say if \(0<|w -z|<\rho\) then \(0<|f(w)-f(z)|<\delta\). Using \(f(w)\) for \(v\), we have if \(0<|w -z|<\rho\) then \(|\frac{g(f(w))-g(f(z))}{f(w)-f(z)} - L| < \epsilon\) as needed. This shows that the limit above exists and equals \(g'(f(z))\).


Corollary 3 If \(g:X \to Y\) (\(X \subseteq {\mathbb C}\), \(Y \subseteq {\mathbb C}\)) is a differentiable bijection with nonzero derivative and continuous right inverse function \(f\) (so \(g \circ f = \operatorname{id}\)). Then \(f\) is also differentiable, and \(f'(z) = \frac{1}{g'(f(z))}\) for all \(z \in Y\).

We would like to apply the previous theorem to square roots, but first we must discuss the square root of a complex number. Notice that any complex number \(z\) can be written in the form \(r \operatorname{cis}(\theta)\), with \(r\geq 0\) and \(\theta \in (-\pi, \pi]\) (or alternatively \([0, 2\pi)\)). Then let \(w = \sqrt{r}\operatorname{cis}(\theta/2)\). Explicitly as a function of \(z\), we have \(w = \sqrt{\left| z \right|} \operatorname{cis}(\arg(z)/2)\), where \(\arg(z)\) is an argument function, or angle, of \(z\). From the properties of the function \(\operatorname{cis}\) (Proposition 3), we see that \(w^2 = z\) and it’s legitimate to write \(w = \sqrt{z}\). Since \((\sqrt{z})^2 = z\), we appear to be in the situation of Theorem 14, but only if we can say \(\sqrt{z}\) is continuous.
Notice that \(\operatorname{cis}(\theta) = \cos(\theta) + i\sin(\theta)\) is continuous by sum and multiple rules, since \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) are continuous. Furthermore \(r = \left| z \right|\) is a continuous function of \(z\), and \(\sqrt{-}\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)\). It follows that \(f(z)=\sqrt{z}\) is continuous whenever \(\arg(z)\) is continuous.

Proposition 16 Let \(\arg:{\mathbb C}- \{0\} \to (-\pi,\pi]\) with \(\arg(r\operatorname{cis}(\theta)) = \theta\) whenever \(\theta \in (-\pi, \pi]\). Then \(\arg\) is continuous at \(z\) when \(\arg(z)\) is in the interior of the range and discontinuous at \(z\) when \(arg(z)\) is on the boundary. The statement remains true if the range \((-\pi, \pi]\) is replaced with any other halfopen interval of length \(2\pi\).


Proof. Let \(\theta_0 = \arg(z)\). If \(\theta_0 \in (-\pi, \pi)\), let \(\arg(z) \in B(\theta_0 , {\varepsilon}) \subseteq (-\pi,\pi)\). Then \(\arg^{-1}(B(\theta_0,{\varepsilon}))\) is the wedge \(\{r \operatorname{cis}(\theta) | \theta \in B(\theta_0 ,{\varepsilon})\}\), which is an open set containing \(z\). On the other hand if \(\arg(z) = \theta_0 = \pi\), then \(z\) is negative real and every neighborhood \(B(z,\delta)\) contains points \(y\) with negative argument, so \(\arg^{-1}(B(\theta_0, 1))\) is not open.
To elaborate, notice that by restriction \(\arg(z):S^1 \to (-\pi, \pi]\). This map has compact domain but noncompact image, so it must be discontinuous somewhere. 

Returning to the square root, we see that \(w = \sqrt{z} = \sqrt{\left| z \right|} \operatorname{cis}(\arg(z)/2)\) is discontinuous exactly when \(z\) is negative real. A technical argument shows that it is continuous at \(z=0\) as well. The derivative formula \(\frac{d}{dz}\sqrt{z} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\) is valid for all \(z\) except negative reals, where \(\sqrt{z}\) is discontinuous, and zero, where \(z^2\) has zero derivative. A different choice of range for \(\arg(z)\) gives a different square root function, but always one discontinuous on an open ray from the origin.

Exercise 29 Recall that the kernel of the \(\operatorname{cis}\) map is known. Let \(w, z \in {\mathbb C}\). By using polar coordinates for \(w\) and \(z\), prove that \(\arg(wz) = \arg(w)+\arg(z) + 2 \pi n\) for some \(n \in {\mathbb Z}\). Here the \(2 \pi n\) term records the inherent ambiguity of angle measure. Except for this term, the law should remind you of a logarithmic function.


Exercise 30 The map \(f(z)=z^2\), restricted to the unit circle \(S^1 = \{z\in {\mathbb C} \,|\, 1=|z|\}\), is a map from \(S^1\) to itself. What is its homotopy class?

title: Complex Analysis
section: 4.2 Cauchy Riemann Equations and Harmonic Functions
text:
4.2 Cauchy Riemann Equations and Harmonic Functions
Because a single complex number determines two real numbers, its real and imaginary part, a function \(f:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\) can be thought of as a function with two real inputs and two real outputs, or even two distinct functions \(u(x,y) = Re(f(x+iy))\) and \(v(x,y) = Im(f(x+iy))\), so that \(f(x+iy) = u(x,y) + i v(x,y)\), where \(u:{\mathbb R}^2 \to {\mathbb R}\) and \(v:{\mathbb R}^2 \to {\mathbb R}\). This perspective is arguably more complicated, but allows us to relate properties of complex functions to the multivariable calculus of real functions. The first application of this line of thinking is called the Cauchy Riemann Equations

Proposition 17 (Cauchy-Riemann Equations) Let \(f(z) = f(x+iy) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y)\) be a complex function differentiable at \(z \in {\mathbb C}\) (where \(u:{\mathbb R}^2 \to {\mathbb R}\) and \(v:{\mathbb R}^2 \to {\mathbb R}\)). Then at \(z\):
\[\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}  \enspace \text{ and } \enspace \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\]


Proof. If the limit \(f'(z) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z+h)-f(z)}{h}\) exists, then it must agree with limits in which the variable \(h\) remains purely real or purely imaginary. So if \(f'(z)\) exists, then
\[f'(z) =  \lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \in {\mathbb R}}} \frac{f(z+h)-f(z)}{h} =  \lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \in {\mathbb R}}} \frac{f(z+ih)-f(z)}{ih}\]
If \(f'(x+iy) = u(x,y) + iv(x,y)\) then each limit is a combination of partial derivatives of \(u\) and \(v\):
\[f'(z) = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + i \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} =  \frac{1}{i} \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + i \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)\]
Setting the real parts equal yields the first Cauchy Riemann equation, and setting imaginary parts equal yields the second. 

If the function \(f:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\) is a twice differentiable, then the Cauchy Riemann equations apply to its derivative \(f'(z) = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + i \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\). This means
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} \enspace \text{ and } \enspace \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}\]
Applying the same to the other formula \(if'(z) = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} + i \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\) produces
