We begin with a geometric series for \(\frac{1}{w-z}\), centered at \(z_0\): \[\frac{1}{w-z} = \frac{1}{(w-z_0) - (z-z_0)} = \frac{1}{w-z_0} \cdot \frac{1}{1-\frac{z-z_0}{w-z_0}} =  \frac{1}{w-z_0} \cdot \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{z-z_0}{w-z_0}\right)^n\] For fixed \(z \in B(z_0,R)\) and all \(w\) on the boundary, \(\left| \frac{z-z_0}{w-z_0} \right|<1\) is constant in \(w\), so we have uniformly convergence \[\begin{align}
f(z) =  \frac{1}{2\pi i }\int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw
    =& \frac{1}{2\pi i }\int_\gamma f(w) \frac{1}{w-z_0} \cdot \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{z-z_0}{w-z_0}\right)^n dw\\
    =& \sum_{n=0}^\infty (z-z_0)^n \frac{1}{2\pi i } \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{(w-z_0)^{n+1}} dw\\
\end{align}\]

This theorem sets complex analysis apart from real analysis more clearly than any other. For real functions the conditions of differentiability, continuous differentiability, twice differentiability, infinite differentiability, etc. are all distinguishable, but this theorem tells us that differentiability on an open set gives us infinite differentiability. It is of course a powerful tool, and we will now see major theorems begin to fall like dominoes.

Theorem 43 Let \(f\) be differentiable on an open set \(U\), and let \(a \in U\). If \(\forall n \enspace f^{(n)}(a)=0\), then \(f\) is constantly zero on a neighborhood of \(a\). Moreover the set \(S\) of points \(a\) for which \(\forall n \enspace f^{(n)}(a)=0\) is clopen. If \(U\) is connected and any such point exists, then \(f=0\) on \(U\).


Proof. Since \(f\) is differentiable on a neighborhood of \(a\), it has a convergent power series with nonzero radius of convergence. Its coefficients \(f^{(n)}(a)/n!\) are all zero, so \(f=0\) on an open neighborhood \(B(a,r)\) of \(a\). Furthermore the power series for \(f\) at any point \(b \in B(a,r)\) is clearly zero as well. This proves that \(S\) is open. Since \(S\) is the intersection of preimages \((f^{(n)})^{-1}(\{0\})\) of closed sets under continuous maps, \(S\) is closed. 


Theorem 44 (Morera’s Theorem) Let \(V \subset {\mathbb C}\) be open, and let \(f\) be continuous on \(V\). If \(\int_{\partial T} f(z) dz=0\) for any triangle \(T \subset V\) then \(f\) is infinitely differentiable.


Proof. On any (convex!) ball \(B(z_0,R) \subseteq V\), \(f\) has a primitive \(F\), and \(F'=f\). Since \(F\) has a power series, it is twice (in fact infinitely) differentiable, so \(f\) is differentiable (infinitely). 


Theorem 45 (Cauchy’s Estimates) Let \(f\) be differentiable on \(\overline{B(z_0,R)}\), and assume \(|f(z)|\leq M\) on the boundary. Then \(\left| f^{(n)}(z_0) \right| \leq \frac{Mn!}{R^n}\).*


Proof. From the power series expansion Theorem 42, we know \(\left| f^{(n)}(z_0) \right| = \left| n!\frac{1}{2\pi i } \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{(w-z_0)^{n+1}} dw \right|\). The ML-inequality bounds the integral by \(n! \frac{1}{2\pi} \frac{M}{R^{(n+1)}} 2 \pi R = \frac{Mn!}{R^n}\). 


A function \(f:{\mathbb C}\to {\mathbb C}\) is called entire if it is defined and differentiable on all of \({\mathbb C}\).


Theorem 46 (Liouville’s Theorem) Any bounded entire function is constant.


Proof. Assume \(\left| f(z) \right| \leq M\) for all \(z\). Fix \(z_0 \in {\mathbb C}\). Then \(\left| f'(z_0) \right| \leq M/R\), for all \(R\), so \(f'(z_0)=0\). Since \(f\) has constant zero derivative (and \({\mathbb C}\) is connected), \(f\) is constant. 

Our next theorem is taught even in high school. It is an old joke that the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra is neither fundamental, nor a theorem of algebra.

Theorem 47 (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra) Let \(P(x) \in {\mathbb C}[x]\) be a nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients. Then \(P\) has a root in \({\mathbb C}\).


Proof. Certainly \(P(z)\) is entire. If \(P(z)\) has no root, then \(1/P(z)\) is also entire. Let \(a_nz^n\) be the leading coefficient. Now \(\left| P(z) \right| = \left| z^n \right|\left| a_n + a_{n-1}z^{-1} + \ldots + a_0z^{-n} \right| \geq \left| z^n \right|(\left| a_n \right| - \left| a_{n-1}z^{-1} \right| - \ldots - \left| a_{0}z^{-n} \right|)\). Whenever \(|z| \geq R = 2n\max(a_i/a_n,1)\), we continue \(P(x) \geq \left| z^n \right|\left(\left| a_n \right| - \frac{\left| a_{n-1}a_n \right|}{2na_{n-1}} - \ldots - \frac{\left| a_{0}a_n \right|}{2na_0} \right) = \left| z^n \right|\left| \frac{a_n}{2} \right| \geq \left| \frac{a_n}{2} \right|\). Thus when \(z \geq R\) we have \(|\frac1{P(z)}| \leq \left| \frac{2}{a_n} \right|\). On the other hand, \(\frac{1}{P(z)}\) is bounded on \(\overline{B(z,R)}\) by continuity (if \(P(z)\) has no roots) and compactness. Thus \(\frac{1}{P(z)}\) is constant and so is \(P(z)\). 

Our next formula can be interpreted as a generalized Pythagorean theorem. It is also significant in Fourier analysis, where it says that the energy in a waveform \(f\) is the sum of the energies represented in each fourier component.

Theorem 48 (Parseval’s Formula) Let \(f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-a)^n\) be a power series with radius of convergence \(R\), and let \(r<R\). Then \[\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \left| f(a+re^{it}) \right|^2 dt = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left| a_nr^n \right|^2\]

Notice the connection with Fourier series: \(f(a+re^{it}) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(re^{it})^n =
\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nr^ne^{int} =\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nr^n (\cos(nt) + i \sin(nt))\), a Fourier series with coefficients \(a_nr^n\).

Proof. Consider the inner product \(\langle f,g \rangle \equiv_\text{def} \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(t)\overline{g(t)}dt\) and functions \(b_n(t) = e^{int}\) for \(n \in {\mathbb N}\). Now \(\int_0^{2\pi} e^{int} dt= \left.\frac{1}{in} e^{int}\right\vert_0^{2\pi}=0\) unless \(n=0\), when \(\int_0^{2\pi} e^{int} dt = 2\pi\). It follows that \(\langle b_m,b_n \rangle = 1\) if \(m=n\) and \(0\) otherwise. The power series expresses \(f(a+re^{it})\) in terms of this basis: \(f(a+re^{it}) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(re^{it})^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nr^n b_n(t)= \lim s_N\), where \(s_N(t) =\sum_{n=0}^N a_nr^n b_n(t)\). Now the convergence \(s_N \to f\) is uniform on \(\overline{B(a,r)}\) since \(r<R\), and the same is true of \(\left| s_N \right|^2 \to \left| f \right|^2\). Therefore \[\begin{align}
    \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \left| f(a+re^{it}) \right|^2 dt
    =& \lim_{N \to \infty}  \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \left| s_N(t) \right|^2 dt\\
    =& \lim_{N \to \infty}\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} s_N(t)\overline{s_N(t)} dt \\
    =& \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \sum_{m=0}^N a_mr^m b_m(t)\overline{\sum_{n=0}^N a_nr^n b_n(t)} dt \\
    =& \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\pi}  \sum_{m=0}^N \sum_{n=0}^N \int_0^{2\pi} a_mr^m b_m(t)\overline{ a_nr^n b_n(t)} dt \\
    =& \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{n=0}^N \left| a_nr^n \right|^2  = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left| a_nr^n \right|^2 \text{ as desired.}\\
\end{align}\]


Theorem 49 (Maximum Modulus Theorem) Let \(f\) be differentiable and nonconstant on a connected open set \(U\). Then \(\left| f \right|\) does not achieve a local maximum on \(U\).


Proof. Let \(a \in U\). On some ball \(B(a,R)\) we have a convergent power series \(f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-a)^n\), and for some smaller ball \(B(a,r)\), Parceval’s formula holds. For some \(n>0\) we have \(a_n \neq 0\) by Theorem 43. Suppose \(\left| f(a+re^{it}) \right| \leq \left| f(a) \right|\) for all \(t\). Then \[|f(a)|^2 = \left| a_0 \right|^2 <  \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left| a_nr^n \right|^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \left| f(a+re^{it}) \right|^2 dt \leq \frac{1}{2\pi} 2\pi \left| f(a) \right|^2 =\left| f(a) \right|^2\] by Theorem 48 and the Theorem 29. This contradiction shows \(a\) cannot be a local maximum of \(\left| f(z) \right|\). 

If we consider a compact domain, such as \(\overline{B(0,R)}\), then of course \(\left| f \right|\) attains a maximum value. The Maximum Modulus Theorem guarantees that it occurs on the boundary.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
6.3 General Cauchy Integral Theorem
The theorems of the previous section testify to the strength of Theorem 41. In this section we will develop a version for more general paths \(\gamma\). We follow Dixon’s approach.
Throughout this section, let \(\gamma:[\alpha,\beta] \to {\mathbb C}\) be a path. We assume \(\gamma\) is continuous, and bounded variation (for example, piecewise smooth). Fix \(a\) and consider \(\int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-a} dw\). Naively we may wish to calculate \(\int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-a} dw = \log(\gamma(\beta))-\log(\gamma(\alpha)) = 0\), but of course this is wrong even for the circular path \(\gamma = z+e^{it}\), because \(\log(w-a)\) is not an antiderivative of \(1/(w-a)\) when \(w-a\in (-\infty,0]\). The next proposition assures us that this wrong calculation is, at worst, off by a multiple of \(2\pi i\).

Let \(a \in {\mathbb C}\). Let \(\gamma:[\alpha,\beta] \to {\mathbb C}- \{a\}\). Then \[\int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-a} dw = \log(\gamma(\beta))-\log(\gamma(\alpha)) + 2 \pi i n\] for some \(n \in {\mathbb Z}\).*


Proof. We consider \(x \in [\alpha,\beta]\). Let \(X\) be the set of all \(x \in [\alpha,\beta]\) for which the theorem is true for \(\gamma\rvert_{[\alpha,x]}\). Now fix \(x_1\). Let \(\gamma(x_1) = z_1\). If \(z_1-a\) is not a negative real, choose \({\varepsilon}>0\) so that \(\log(w-a)\) is continuous on \(B(z_1, {\varepsilon})\) and \(\delta>0\) so that \(\gamma(B(x_1,\delta)) \subseteq B(z_1, {\varepsilon})\). Let \(x_2 \in B(x_1,\delta)\). Let \(\gamma_1 = \gamma\rvert_{[\alpha,x_1]}\), \(\gamma_2 = \gamma\rvert_{[\alpha,x_2]}\), and \(\gamma_\Delta = \gamma\rvert_{[x_1,x_2]}\), so \(\int_{\gamma_2} = \int_{\gamma_1} +\int_{\gamma_\Delta}\) Now \(\log\) is an antiderivative for the integral \(\int_{\gamma_\Delta} \frac{1}{w-a} dz = \log(\gamma(x_2)) - \log(\gamma(x_1))\). Thus the theorem statement is true for \(x_1\) if and only if it is true for \(x_2\).
Now if \(z_1-a\) is a negative real, consider the function \(\log'(z) = \ln(\left| z \right|) + i \arg'(z)\), where \(\arg'(z) \in [0,2\pi)\). Then \(\log'(z) - \log(z) \in \{0, 2\pi i \}\). Moreover, \(\log'(w-a)\) is an antiderivative of \(\frac{1}{w-a}\) unless \(w-a\) is a positive real. Using \(\log'\) in place of \(\log\), the above argument goes through again.
We conclude that \(x_1 \in X\) iff \(x_2 \in X\). This shows that \(X\) is both open and closed. Since \(\alpha \in X\), we deduce \(\beta \in X\) as desired. 

In the case of a closed curve \(\gamma\), \(\log(\gamma(\beta))-\log(\gamma(\alpha))=0\). The number \(n\) simply counts the number of times \(\gamma\) winds around \(z\) in the counterclockwise direction. We cannot assert this as a theorem without the algebraic topology to define “winds”, so instead we take it as a definition:

Let \(a \in {\mathbb C}\). Let \(\gamma:[\alpha,\beta] \to {\mathbb C}- \{a\}\), \(v(\gamma)<\infty\). The Winding number of \(\gamma\) around \(a\) is: \[n(\gamma, a) \equiv_{def} \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-a} dw\]


For fixed \(\gamma\) with \(v(\gamma)<\infty\), the winding number \(W(\gamma,z)\) is a locally constant function of \(z \in {\mathbb C}- im(\gamma)\).


Proof. This is essentially a continuity argument. Fix \(z \notin im(\gamma)\). Since \(\gamma\) is continuous, \(im(\gamma)\) is compact, so closed. Let \(B(z,{\varepsilon}_1)\) be disjoint from \(\gamma\), and consider \({\varepsilon}_2<{\varepsilon}_1\) to be decided. Let \(z' \in B(z,{\varepsilon}_1)\). Then \[W(\gamma,z) - W(\gamma,z') = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-z}- \frac{1}{w-z'} dw = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\gamma} \frac{z-z'}{(w-z)(w-z')}dw\] This integral can be bounded above (ML inequality) by \(\frac{v(\gamma) {\varepsilon}_2}{2\pi {\varepsilon}_1^2}\). For sufficiently small \({\varepsilon}_2<{\varepsilon}_1\), this is less than \(1\), so the \(W(\gamma,z) - W(\gamma,z') =0\) as desired. 

Here’s another proof, arguably a better proof:

Proof. It suffices to show that \(\int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-z} dw\) is a locally constant function of \(z\), so let \(z, z' \in B(z, {\varepsilon})\), where \(B(z,{\varepsilon})\) lies in one component of \({\mathbb C}- \{\gamma\}\). Then \[\int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-z} dw - \int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-z'} dw = \int_{\gamma} \frac{1}{w-z}-\frac{1}{w-z'} dw\] As we’ve proved earlier, this integrand has an antiderivative \(\log\left(\frac{w-z}{w-z'} \right)\) everywhere except the line segment connecting \(z\) to \(z'\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integral is zero. 

We take for granted that the complement of a path \({\mathbb C}- im(\gamma)\) has exactly one unbounded component. A path \(\gamma\) can’t wind around a point in that component. This is obvious geometrically, but not from our integral definition.

Theorem 50 If \(\gamma: [\alpha,\beta] \to {\mathbb C}\), with \(v(\gamma)<\infty\). Let \(z\) be in the unbounded component of \({\mathbb C}-im(\gamma)\). Then \(W(\gamma,z)=0\).


Proof. By local constancy, \(W(\gamma,z)\) is constant on the component of interest. When \(z\) is sufficiently far from \(im(\gamma)\), (distance \(\geq M\), say) we have \(\left| \frac{1}{w-z} \right| < 1/M\), so \(\left| W(\gamma,z) \right| \leq \frac{v(\gamma)}{2\pi M}\). For \(M\) sufficiently large, this is close to \(0\), so equal to \(0\). Since \(W(\gamma,z)\) is constant for such \(z\), \(W(\gamma,z)=0\) for all \(z\) in the component.

title: Complex Analysis
text:
6.4 Singularities
We turn our attention to singularities of a function \(f\) – points where \(f\) fails to be defined. Properties of singularities \(z_0\) depend not on \(f(z_0)\), which does not exist, but on \(f(z)\) for \(z\) nearby \(z_0\).

Definition 5.25. Let \(z_0 \in {\mathbb C}\).

A deleted neighborhood of \(z_0\) is a set of the form \(U-\{z_0\}\), where \(z_0 \in U\) and \(U\) is open.
A singularity of a function \(f\) is a point \(z_0\) so that \(f(z_0)\) is analytic on a deleted neighborhood of \(z_0\) but undefined or not analytic at \(z_0\).
If \(z_0 \in {\mathbb C}\), the phrase near \(z_0\) means “on some deleted neighborhood of \(z_0\). For example,”\(f\) is constant near \(z_0\)” means there is some open set \(U \ni z\) for which \(f|_{U -\{z_0\}}\) is constant.


Notice that by definition a singularity \(a\) is isolated in the sense that some neighborhood of \(a\) has no singularities.

Some common singularities.

The function \[f(z) = \frac{e^z}{(z-3)^2}\] is undefined at \(z_0=3\). As \(z\) approaches \(3\), the numerator approaches \(e^3 \approx 20.1\) and the denominator approaches \(0\), so the fraction is unbounded. Thus, there is no value which can be assigned to \(f(3)\) which makes it continuous at \(3\). We call this singularity a pole of order 2.
The function \[g(z) = \frac{z^2-9}{(z-3)}\] is undefined at \(z_0=3\). For all \(z \neq z_0\), we have \(g(z) = z+3\). We call this singularity removable because the function can be assigned a value at \(z_0\) which repairs the problem.
The function \[h(z) = \frac{(z-3)^2(z-4)^2}{(z-3)}\] is undefined at \(z_0=3\). Again we can cancel, removing the singularity. In this case the resulting function has a root at \(3\).
The function \[k(z) = e^{1/z}\] is undefined at \(z_0=0\). As \(z\) approaches \(z_0=0\), the exponent goes to infinity. Because the exponent goes to infinity, the function \(k(z)\) goes to infinity very quickly and has some strange properties. This is an example of an essential singularity.



Let \(f\) have a singularity at \(z_0\). If there is some value \(w\) such that the function \[\hat{f}(z) = \begin{cases} f(z) & z \neq z_0 \\ w & z = z_0 \end{cases}\]
is analytic at \(z_0\), we call \(z_0\) a removable singularity of \(f\).


(Riemann Continuation Theorem) If \(z_0\) is a singularity of \(f\) and \(f\) is bounded near \(z_0\), then \(z_0\) is removable.


Proof. \[\text{Let } g(z) = \begin{cases} f(z)(z-a)^2 & z \neq a\\ 0 & z=0 \end{cases}\] If \(z \neq z_0\) then \(g'(z)\) can be calculated by the product rule. \(g'(z_0) = \lim_{z \to z_0} f(z)(z-z_0) = 0\) since \(z-z_0 \to 0\) and \(f(z)\) is bounded near \(z_0\). It follows that \(g\) has a power series expansion \(g(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n\), and \(a_0=a_1=0\). We may divide by \((z-z_0)^2\) termwise to find a power series expansion for \(f(z)\) centered at \(a\). 

The Riemann Continuation Theorem means that complex function theory has nothing like the “jump discontinuities” from ordinary real Calculus.
Roots and Poles should be understood as opposites, but first we need to understand functions which have neither:

Let \(g\) be analytic on a neighborhood of \(z_0\). (So \(z_0\) is not a singularity of \(g\).) Then the following are equivalent:

\(g(z_0) \neq 0\)
\(1/g\) is analytic on some (possibly smaller) neighborhood of \(z_0\)
The power series expansion of \(g\) at \(z_0\) is of the form \(g(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n\) with \(a_0 \neq 0\).



Proof. From prior work, \(f\) has a power series expansion with positive radius of convergence, and \(f(z_0) = a_0\). Thus \(1 \leftrightarrow 3\) follows. Moreover \(2 \to 1\) is obvious. For \(1 \to 2\), note that \(f\) is nonzero on some neighborhood \(z_0\) by continuity, and on this neighborhood \(1/f\) is analytic by the quotient rule. 


Let \(f\) be analytic on a neighborhood of \(z_0\). If \(f(z) = (z-z_0)^kg(z)\) (for positive integer \(k\)) and \(g(z_0) \neq 0\), we call \(z_0\) a root of order \(k\) of \(f\).


Let \(f\) be analytic near \(z_0\). If \(f(z) = (z-z_0)^{-k}g(z)\) (for positive integer \(k\)) and \(g(z_0) \neq 0\), we call \(z_0\) a pole of order \(k\) of \(f\).


Let \(f\) be analytic near \(z_0\). The valuation \(v_{z_0}(f)\) of \(f\) at \(z_0\) is defined to be \[v_{z_0}(f) = \begin{cases} 0 &  \text{$f$ if analytic at $z_0$ and $f(z_0) \neq 0$}\\ k &  \text{$f$ has a root of order $k$ at $z_0$.}\\ -k &  \text{$f$ has a pole of order $k$ at $z_0$.}\\ \infty &  \text{$f=0$ on a neighborhood of $z_0$.}\\ \text{(undefined)} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]


Let \(f\) be analytic near \(z_0\).

If \(f\) has a root of order \(k\) at \(z_0\) then \(f\) has power series expansion at \(z_0\): \[f(z) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n\] and \(a_k \neq 0\) is the first nonzero coefficient.
If \(f\) has a pole of order \(k\) at \(z_0\) then near \(z_0\), \(f\) can be written \[f(z) = \sum_{n=-k}^\infty a_n(z-z_0)^n\] and \(a_{-k} \neq 0\). This is called the Laurent Series Expansion of \(f\) at \(z_0\).
If \(f\) has a root (pole) of order \(k\) at \(z_0\) then \(1/f\) has a pole (root) of order \(k\) at \(z_0\)
\(v_{z_0}(f)\) is the index of the first nonzero term in the Laurent (or power) series expansion of \(f\).
\(v_{z_0}(fg) = v_{z_0}(f) v_{z_0}(g)\) if the right hand side is defined.



Proof. Directly from the definitions, using properties of \(g\) proved above. 

Just as locally bounded functions must have removable singularities, functions which become locally bounded when multiplied by \((z-z_0)^k\) must have poles:

If \(f\) is not bounded near \(a\), but \(f(z)(z-z_0)^k\) is bounded near \(z_0\) for some \(k\), and if \(k\) is minimal with this property, then \(f\) has a pole of order \(k\) at \(z_0\).


Proof. After multiplying by \((z-z_0)^k\) we may invoke the Riemann Continuation theorem. Subsequently dividing by \((z-z_0)^k\) we get a Laurent series whose first nonzero term is \(a_{-k}(z-z_0)^{-k}\), which indicates a pole of order \(k\). The coefficient \(a_{-k}\) is nonzero by the minimality of \(k\). 


Let \(U \subset {\mathbb C}\) be open. A meromorphic function on \(U\) is a function \(f\) analytic on \(U\) except on a set of points where \(f\) has poles. (Of course \(f\) may also have zeroes.) The set of all meromorphic functions on \(U\) is written \({\mathcal M}(U)\).


Let \(U \subset {\mathbb C}\) be open. Then \({\mathcal M}(U)\) is a field under function addition and multiplication.


Proof. We know that function addition and multiplication obey the field axioms. The point of the proposition is to identify additive and multiplicative identities and prove that if \(f\) and \(g\) are meromorphic, then so are \(-f\), \(f+g\), \(fg\). Also, if \(g \neq 0\) then \(1/g\) must be meromorphic. Each part makes a nice exercise. Work locally at each singularity \(z_0\). 

We have described functions bounded near \(z_0\), which have removable singularities. We have described functions that become bounded only when multiplied by \((z-z_0)^k\), which have poles. The next theorem addresses the only other case. It describes the most exotic type of singularity.

(Casorati-Weierstrass) If \(f(z)(z-z_0)^n\) is not bounded near \(z_0\) for any \(n\), then \(f(B(z_0,{\varepsilon}))\) is dense in \({\mathbb C}\) for every \({\varepsilon}>0\). In this case we say that \(f\) has an essential singularity.


Proof. If \(f(B(z_0,{\varepsilon})-\{z_0\})\) is not dense, choose an open ball \(B(b, \delta)\) disjoint from its image. Then the function \(g(z) = \frac{1}{f(z)-b}\) is analytic and nonzero on \(B(z_0,{\varepsilon}) - \{z_0\}\) and bounded above by \(1/\delta\). Since \(g\) is bounded it may be continued to \(z_0\) (so we assume \(g(z_0)\) exists). Solving for \(f\) gives: \[f(z) = \frac{1}{g(z)} + b\] Thus \(f\) is meromorphic on some neighborhood of \(B(z_0, {\varepsilon})\). It follows that \(f(z)(z-z_0)^n\) is bounded near \(z_0\) for some \(n\). This proves (the contrapositive of) the claim. 


6.4.1 Generalized Cauchy Integral Formula

Let \(g(z,w)\) be a continuous function of \(z\) and \(w\) on a domain \(U \times V\), analytic in \(z\) for each \(w\). Assume \(U\) is open and \(V\) is locally compact. Then the partial derivative function \(\frac{\partial}{\partial z} g(z,w) = g_z(z,w)\) is likewise a continuous function of two variables. (and of course analytic in \(z\))


Proof. Fix \(z_0\) and \(w_0\).
Case 1: Assume \(g(z_0,w_0) = g_z(z_0,w_0)=0\). By the definition of \(g_z\) we have \(\lim_{z \to z_0} \frac{g(z,w_0)}{z-z_0}=0\). Let \({\varepsilon}>0\) and choose \(r\) so that \(\overline{B(z_0,2r)} \subseteq U\) and whenever \(\left| z-z_0 \right| \leq 2r\) then \(\left| \frac{g(z,w_0)}{z-z_0} \right|<{\varepsilon}/2\). Thus on \(B(z_0,2r) \times \{w_0\}\) we have \(|g(z,w)| < r{\varepsilon}/2\) Notice that Cauchy’s bound for \(f'(z)\) says \(\left| g_z(z_0,w_0) \right| \leq \frac{\frac{r{\varepsilon}}{2} 1!}{r} = {\varepsilon}/2\), which of course we already knew. We wish to extend this bound to a neighborhood of \((z_0,w_0)\). On the compact region \(\overline{B(z_0,2r)} \times \overline{B(w_0,r)}\) choose \(\delta>0\) (with also \(\delta<r\)) for \(r {\varepsilon}/2\) in the uniform continuity of \(g\). We imagine an annulus in \(U\) with radii \(r-\delta\) and \(r+\delta\), given a thickness \(2\delta\) in the \(V\)-direction. It follows by the triangle inequality that if \(r-\delta < \left| z-z_0 \right| < r+\delta\) and \(\left| w-w_0 \right|<\delta\) then \(|g(z,w)| = \left| g(z,w) - g(z,w_0) + g(z,w_0) \right| \leq  \left| g(z,w) - g(z,w_0) \right| + \left| g(z,w_0) \right| <r{\varepsilon}\). This bounds \(g\) along the boundary of any ball (in the \(U\)-direction) of radius \(r\) around any \((z_1, w_1)\) in the neighborhood \(B(z_0, \delta) \times B(w_0, \delta)\). Then for any such \((z_1, w_1)\), Cauchy’s bound gives \(\left| g_z(z_1,w_1) \right|<{\varepsilon}\) as desired. This shows that \(g\) is a continuous function of two variables at \(z_0, w_0\) in this case.
Case 2: Apply Case 1 to the function \(g(z,w) - g_z(z_0,w_0)(z-z_0) - g(z_0,w_0)\), a function of \(z\) and \(w\) whose partial with respect to \(z\) is \(g_z(z,w) - g_z(z_0,w_0)\). This shows that \(g_z(w,z)\) plus a constant is continuous, thus so is \(g_z(w,z)\). 


(Leibniz Integral Formula) Let \(g(z, w)\) a continuous function of two variables, and analytic in \(z\) for each \(w\). Let \(\gamma\) be a continuous, bounded variation path. Then \[\frac{d}{dz} \int_\gamma g(z,w) dw = \int_\gamma g_z(z,w) dw\]


Proof. Fix \(z_0\). For each \(w\) consider the tangent line approximation \(g(z,w) = g_z(z_0,w)(z-z_0) + g(z_0,w) + e(z,w)\) where \(\lim_{z \to z_0} \frac{e(z,w) }{z-z_0} = 0\). By the previous lemma, \(g_z(z_0,w)\) is a continuous function of \(w\), so \(e(z,w)\) is a continuous function of \(z\) and \(w\). \[\left(\frac{d}{dz} \int_\gamma g(z,w) dw \right) - \int_\gamma g_z(z,w) dw = \lim_{z \to z_0} \left[\frac{\int_\gamma g(z,w) dw - \int_\gamma g(z_0,w) dw}{z-z_0} - \int_\gamma g_z(z_0,w) dw \right] = \lim_{z \to z_0} \int_\gamma \frac{e(z,w)}{z-z_0} dw\] On a compact region \(\overline{B(z_0,{\varepsilon})} \times im(\gamma)\), the function \(e\) is uniformly continuous, and by Corollary 11 the limit commutes with the integral: \[\lim_{z \to z_0} \int_\gamma \frac{e(z,w)}{z-z_0} dw = \int_\gamma \lim_{z \to z_0} \frac{e(z,w)}{z-z_0} dw= 0\] 


Let \(U \subseteq {\mathbb C}\) be open. Let \(\gamma\) be a closed path in \(U\). We call \(\gamma\) homologous to zero in \(U\) if \(W(\gamma, a)=0\) for all \(a \notin U\).


(Cauchy Integral Formula, general case) Let \(U \subseteq {\mathbb C}\) be open, and let \(\gamma\) be homologous to zero in \(U\). Let \(f\) be analytic on \(U\). Then for all \(z \in U\) \[\int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw = 2\pi i W(\gamma,z) f(z)\]


Proof. Now consider a path \(\gamma\) and a function \(f\). Write \(E\) for the union of the components of \({\mathbb C}- \{\gamma\}\) on which \(W(\gamma,z)=0\). Notice that \(E\) includes the unbounded component of \({\mathbb C}- \{\gamma\}\), by Theorem 50. Let us assume \(f\) is differentiable on \(U\), and \(U \cup E = {\mathbb C}\). As before, \[\text{let } q(z,w) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z}  & \text{ if $w \neq z$} \\ f'(z)& \text{ if $w= z$} \end{array} \right.\] Since \(f\) is differentiable, it is continuously so, and \(q\) is uniformly continuous on any compact set. For fixed \(z\), \(q(z,w)\) is a differentiable function of \(w\) and continuous at \(w=z\), where it therefore has a removable singularity. Thus \(q\) is analytic in each variable separately. \[\text{Let } h(z) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \int_\gamma q(z,w) dw  & \text{ if $z \in U$} \\[1em] \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw &\text{if $z \in E$} \end{array}\right.\] On the (open!) overlap \(U \cap E\), these agree because \(\int_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{w-z}=0\) by assumption. We claim \(h(z)\) is entire. On \(U\), the Leibniz rule applies and \(h'(z) = \frac{d}{dz} \int_\gamma q(z,w) dw = \int_{\gamma} q_z(z,w) dw\). Notice \(q_z\) is a continuous function \(w\), in fact of two variables, so the integral exists, so \(h'\) exists.
On \(E - U\), Leibniz rule gives \(\frac{d}{dz} \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw = \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{(w-z)^2} dw\). Again this is continuous since \(w \neq z\) for \(w \in \{\gamma\}\).
However, for \(z\) sufficiently far from the compact set \(\{\gamma\}\) (say when \(d(z, \{\gamma\})>R\)) we bound \(h(z) = \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw\) by ML: \[\left| \int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw \right| \leq \max_{w \in \{\gamma\}} \left| f(w) \right| \frac{1}{R}\left| v(\gamma) \right|\] That is, \(h\) is bounded for \(\{z\in {\mathbb C}| d(z, \{\gamma\})>R\}\), and bounded on \(\{z\in {\mathbb C}| d(z, \{\gamma\})\leq R\}\) by compactness. It follows that \(h\) is constant. Since \(R\) is arbitrary in the bound \(\left| f(w) \right| \frac{1}{R}\left| v(\gamma) \right|\), \(h\) is the zero function.
Therefore, for all \(z \in U\), we have \[\int_\gamma \frac{f(w)-f(z)}{w-z} dw=0\]
That is, \[\int_\gamma \frac{f(w)}{w-z} dw=\int_\gamma \frac{f(z)}{w-z} dw = 2 \pi i f(z) W(\gamma,z)\] 


Let \(U \subseteq {\mathbb C}\) be open, and let \(f\) be analytic on \(U\), \(\gamma\) closed and homologous to zero in \(U\). Then \(\int_\gamma f(w) dw=0\).


Proof. \(f(w) = f(w)(w-z) / (w-z)\). 


Let \(U \subseteq {\mathbb C}\) be open, and let \(f\) be meromorphic on \(U\), \(\gamma\) closed and homologous to zero in \(U\). Then \(\int_\gamma f(w) dw=2\pi i \sum_i W(\gamma,z_i) Res(f,z_i)\).


Proof. Subtract off higher negative power terms b/c they have antiderivatives. Subtract \(\prod R_i/(w-z_i)\) and remove singularities to produce analytic function. Apply previous corollary.

title: Complex Analysis
section: 6.5 Using the method of residues to calculate real integrals
text:
6.5 Using the method of residues to calculate real integrals
The residue theorem is so powerful that it can solve many ordinary real integrals, particularly improper ones:

We calculate \(\displaystyle \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx\).
With some familiarity with inverse trigonometric functions, one calculates the integral as \(\lim_{b \to \infty} \arctan(b)-\arctan(0) = \pi/2\). In contrast, complex analysis solves the problem without leaving the domain of rational functions.
First we notice that the function is even and has residues at \(i\) and \(-i\). We double the integral to produce the more convenient problem \(\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx\), replace it with the finite version \(\displaystyle \int_{-R}^R \frac{1}{1+x^2} dx\), and regard this straight line real integral as the lower part of a path integral on \(\gamma\), a path which proceeds from \(-R\) to \(R\) along the real line, and then from \(R\) to \(-R\) along a complex upper semicircle centered at \(0\). If we can calculate both the residue at \(i\) (interior to this path) and the integral along the semicircle, we can deduce the straight line integral from Cauchy’s integral formula. The residue at \(i\) is \(\lim_{z \to i}(z-i)\frac{1}{1+z^2} = \lim_{z \to i} \frac{1}{z+i} = \frac1{2i}\). The semicircular integral is harder to calculate, but the ML inequality bounds it at \(\frac{2 \pi R}{R^2-1}\), which goes to zero at \(R\) goes to infinity. In the limit, then, we have
\[\lim_{R \to \infty} \int_{-R}^R \frac{1}{1+z^2} dz = 2 \pi i \frac{1}{2i} = \pi\]
Remember we have doubled the original problem, so the answer is \(\pi/2\) as expected from trigonometry.


We calculate \(\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{1+x^4} dx\). It’s possible to factor this into two irreducible quadratics, complete squares, and apply trigonometric substitutions, but it’s not fun. Instead we integrate as above. Again the semicircular integral is approaches zero, so we have
\[\lim_{R \to \infty} \int_{-R}^R \frac{1}{1+z^4} dz = 2 \pi i (\text{sum of residues})\]
So we need the poles and residues. The roots are \(z^4+1\) are \(e^{\frac14\pi i }\), \(e^{\frac34\pi i }\), \(e^{\frac54\pi i }\), and \(e^{\frac74\pi i }\). Setting \(\alpha = e^{\frac14\pi i }\), we write \(\alpha^3\), \(\alpha^5\), and \(\alpha^7\). Only \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha^3\) are in the upper half plane, so we calculate the residues there. Note of course \(\alpha^4 = -1\).
\[\begin{align}
    \lim_{z \to \alpha} (z-\alpha) \frac{1}{z^4+1} &= \lim_{z \to \alpha}  \frac{(z-\alpha)}{(z-\alpha)(z-\alpha^3)(z-\alpha^5)(z-\alpha^7)} \\
    &= \lim_{z \to \alpha} \frac{1}{(z-\alpha^3)(z-\alpha^5)(z-\alpha^7)} \\
    &= \frac{1}{(\alpha-\alpha^3)(\alpha-\alpha^5)(\alpha-\alpha^7)} \\
    &= \frac{1}{\alpha^3(1-\alpha^2)(1-\alpha^4)(1-\alpha^6)} \\
    &= \frac{\alpha}{(-1)(1-i)(2)(1+i)} \\
    &= \frac{-\alpha}{4}
\end{align}\]
A sneakier calculation is to recognize the limit \(\lim_{z \to \alpha} (z-\alpha) \frac{1}{z^4+1}\) as the reciprocal of the derivative of \(f(z) = z^4+1\) at \(z=\alpha\), which is \(4 \alpha^3\). The reciprocal is \(-\alpha/4\). SImilarly, the residue at \(\alpha^3\) is the reciprocal of \(4\alpha^{9} = 4 \alpha\), or \(-\alpha^3/4\). The sum of the residues is \(\frac{-1}4(\alpha + \alpha^3) =
\frac{-\alpha}4(1+\alpha^2) = \frac{-\alpha}4(1+i) = \frac{-\alpha \sqrt{2}\alpha}{4} = \frac{-\sqrt{2}i}{4}\). We conclude:
\[\lim_{R \to \infty} \int_{-R}^R \frac{1}{1+4^2} dz = 2 \pi i \frac{-\sqrt{2}i}{4} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}\]

4 Appendices

4.1 AI Policy:
Students are encouraged to leverage AI tools, such as Jupyter with code completion features or chatbots for learning help, to enhance their understanding of mathematical concepts and streamline computational tasks. All interactions with AI systems are consultations with an external source, just like a book or another person. Copying the work of an AI system and submitting it as ones own, even with some changes, is a form of plagiarism. Calling on AI for solutions to assigned problems is cheating, for the same reason that hiring your Mom to do your homework is cheating.


4.2 Accommodative Services
Students who need accommodations to complete the requirements and expectations of this course because of a disability should contact the Office of Accommodative Services (136 Sisson Hall, (315) 267-2590, oas@potsdam.edu) or complete their request by filling out the New Student Accommodation Request Form. Please note that accommodations are generally not provided retroactively so timely contact with the Office of Accommodative Services is important. Students registered with the Office of Accommodative Services (OAS) should use the Accommodate Portal to submit their “Semester Request” (Letter of Accommodation) every semester. This letter informs faculty of potential course access and accommodations that might be necessary and reasonable. Further conversation with OAS, faculty, and the student may be warranted to ensure reasonable accommodations.


4.3 Counseling Services
As a student at SUNY Potsdam, you may encounter various stressors that can affect your learning and academic performance. The College Counseling Center (CCC) offers a range of resources to support students in their mental health, social well-being, and overall academic experience. Students seeking to speak with a licensed mental health professional can access free services through the SUNY Potsdam Counseling Center. To connect with our services, please call 315-267-2330, email counseling@potsdam.edu, or visit us at Van Housen 131.


4.4 Disruptive Student Policy
In order to maintain a fair, just, and safe College community environment, students are subject to SUNY Potsdam College regulations and are expected to abide by the Potsdam Pledge, the SUNY Potsdam Academic Catalog, and the Student Community Rights and Responsibilities (the Student Code of Conduct). Anyone who disrupts the academic learning environment (e.g., classrooms, labs, office hours, online platforms, emails, or other virtual communications) will be asked to leave for the day. Disruptions may include, but are not limited to, interrupting/speaking over other people, excessive use of foul or abusive or derogatory language, and repeated getting up/leaving/returning behavior. Students who exhibit aggressive/violent behavior in or out of classrooms will be asked to immediately leave. Disruptive students may be subject to disciplinary action, potentially including administrative removal from the course.


4.5 Food Insecurity
The Prometheus Alumni Food Pantry is in 119 Barrington Student Union. The hours of operation can be found on their Facebook page or Get Involved. An Initial Intake is required 3 of all visitors. Additionally, if you are living off campus and in need of supplemental food assistance, you may be eligible for SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) benefits. To determine eligibility and to enroll, you can visit mybenefits.ny.gov or call Maximizing Independent Living Choices (MILC) at 315-764-9442 x405. The campus has a registered dietician to assist you; you can contact them through the Student Health Services student portal on BearPaws. If you have questions on any of these services or need further assistance, reach out to the Bear CARE Program.


4.6 Land Acknowledgement
We acknowledge with respect the Mohawk Nation, the Indigenous people on whose ancestral lands SUNY Potsdam now stands. We are reminded by our presence here that we have the duty to live in harmony with one another and with all of creation. We are deeply grateful to the families and communities who care for this beautiful place. Beginning with colonization and continuing for centuries the Haudenosaunee Peoples have been dispossessed of most of their ancestral lands by the actions of individuals and institutions. We acknowledge our responsibility to understand and respond to those actions and to commit to working together to honor our past and build our future with truth. For more information on Land Acknowledgements, see Land_Acknowledgement at illuminative.org


4.7 Success Statement
Success in this course depends heavily on your personal health and wellbeing. Recognize that stress is an expected part of the college experience, and it often can be compounded by unexpected setbacks or life changes outside the classroom. I strongly encourage you to reframe challenges as an unavoidable pathway to success. Reflect on your role in taking care of yourself throughout the term, before the demands of exams and projects reach their peak. Please feel free to reach out to me about any difficulty you may be having that may impact your performance in your courses or campus life as soon as it occurs and before it becomes too overwhelming. In addition, I strongly encourage you to contact the many other support services on campus that stand ready to assist you including the Counseling Center & the Case Manager, Student Health Services, Accommodative Services, and your academic advisor.


4.8 Student Support
Every student in this class is a valued individual. If you are struggling with issues outside of the classroom, please know that there are professionals both on and off campus who can assist you. If you need immediate assistance, please contact our campus Counseling Center (with free counseling) at (315) 267-2330 or visit their website. Links to other resources are provided below: • Title IX Coordinator, Van Housen Extension 392, (315) 267-2516, • Bias Incident Reporting • Center for Diversity, 223 Sisson Hall, (315) 267-2184 • University Police, Van Housen Extension, (315) 267-2222 (number for non-emergencies; for an emergency please dial 911) • Student Conduct and Community Standards, 208 Barrington Student Union, • Reachout (24-hour crisis hotline), (315) 265-2422 • Renewal House (for victims of domestic violence), SUNY Potsdam Campus Office: Van Housen Extension 390 (open Wednesdays, 9-5:00), (315) 379-9845 (24-hour crisis hotline), Renewalhouse_campus@Verizon.net • Career Services, Lougheed Learning Commons
And please: if you see something, say something. If you see that someone that you care about is struggling, please encourage them to seek help. If they are unwilling to do so, Care Enough to Call has guidelines on whom to contact. Everyone has the responsibility of creating a college climate of compassion.

title: Homework Problems
text:
Prove parts 8 and 9 from the list of properties in section 1.4 of the notes.



Let \({\mathbb R}[x]\) be the ring of polynomials with real coefficients, let \(c \in {\mathbb R}\), and let \(e_c:{\mathbb R}[x] \to {\mathbb R}\) be the evaluation map at \(c\): \(e_c(p) = p(c)\).

Demonstrate that \(e_c\) is a ring homomorphism.
Calculate the image of \(e_c\), and prove that your answer is correct.
Calculate the kernel of \(e_c\), and prove that your answer is correct.




Let \(f:R \to S\) be a homomorphism of rings. Prove that \(\ker(f) = \{0_R\}\) if and only if \(f\) is injective.



Let \({\mathbb C}\) be the ring of complex numbers, and let \(R = \left \{\begin{bmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{bmatrix}\,\,|\,\, a, b \in {\mathbb R}\right\}\).

For each ring, identify its zero and one. For each ring, define its addition and multiplication operations.
Define a map \(f:{\mathbb C} \to R\) and prove that it is a ring homomorphism.
Calculate the image and kernel of \(f\).




Give an example of each type of element in each ring, or state “impossible.” No need for proof.












\({\mathbb R}\)
\({\mathbb Z}\)
\({\mathbb Z}_{10}\)
\(M^{2 \times 2}_{\mathbb R}\)
\({\mathbb R}[x]\)




A unit (other than 1) in







A nilpotent in







A zerodivisor in







An irreducible in











Interpret this problem in \({\mathbb Z}[x]\), in \({\mathbb R}[x]\), in \({\mathbb C}[x]\), and in \({\mathbb Z}[i][x]\). You should get a variety of answers depending on the ring.
Is \(5x^2 + 5\) an irreducible element of the ring? If so, explain why. If possible, factor it into irreducible elements.



In this problem we explore the ring \(R = {\mathbb Z}[\sqrt{-5}] = \{a + b \sqrt{-5} | a, b \in {\mathbb Z}\}\).

Identify the \(0\) and \(1\) of \(R\). Prove (based on the definition above) that \(R\) is closed under addition and multiplication. Use the subring test to deduce that \(R\) is a subring of \({\mathbb C}\).
To describe the units of \(R\), we need something like a length function on it: For \(a+b\sqrt{-5} \in R\), we define \(\|a+b\sqrt{-5}\|^2 = a^2+5b^2\). (Note that this is just the complex square norm function restricted to \(R\).)


Explain why \(\| - \|^2\) is integer valued.
Prove that \(\Vert v \Vert^2\) is multiplicative in the sense \(\Vert vw\Vert^2 = \Vert v\Vert^2\Vert w\Vert^2\)
Prove (from the previous) that if \(v\) is a unit of \(R\), then \(\|v\|^2 = 1\).


Identify all units of \(R\).
Once units are identified, we can prove that certain elements are irreducible. Demonstrate that \(2\), \(3\), \(1+\sqrt{-5}\), and \(1-\sqrt{-5}\) are all irreducible.
It will perhaps bother you to see that \(2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5}) \cdot(1-\sqrt{-5})\). Among these irreducible factors of six, are any of them unit multiples of others? Why or why not?




Let \(I \subseteq J \subseteq R\), where \(I\) and \(J\) are ideals and \(R\) is a ring. Define \(J/I\) to be \(\{j+I | j \in J\}\).

Prove that \(J/I\) is an ideal of \(R/I\).
Prove that \((R/I) / (J/I)\) is isomorphic to \(R/J\).




Find an infinite repeating pattern of points which, when removed from the lattice \({\mathbb Z}[i]\), do not permit five points in a row, horizontally, vertically, or diagonally, to be found among the remaining points. Minimize the number of points which must be removed.

What proportion of the points of \({\mathbb Z}[i]\) must be removed to exclude five-in-a-row?
Sketch a picture of the points which must be removed.
It’s possible to choose your points so that they correspond to an ideal \(I\) of \({\mathbb Z}[i]\). Is it principal? What is its generator?




Prove that \(R = {\mathbb Z}[x]/(x)\) is isomorphic to \({\mathbb Z}\)



Let \(R\) be a ring and let \(f \in R\) be a nonzero nonnilpotent element. Let \(S = \{1, f, f^2, f^3, \ldots\}\). Let \(P\) be an ideal maximal among all ideals of \(R\) disjoint from \(S\). Prove that \(P\) is a prime ideal. (Hint: Don’t try to prove that \(P\) is maximal.)




Give an example of a ring homomorphism \(f:R \to S\) and a prime ideal \(P\) of \(R\), so that the extension \(P^e\) is the unit ideal.
Give an example of a ring homomorphism \(f:R \to S\) and a prime ideal \(P\) of \(R\), so that the extension \(P^e\) is a proper ideal (i.e., not the unit ideal), but is not prime.




The notes give a rather roundabout demonstration that every maximal ideal \(I\) of a commutative ring \(R\) is prime. It depends on reasoning about the quotient \(R/I\). Give a direct proof that every maximal ideal is prime, without resorting to the quotient ring \(R/I\).



Prove this proposition, which is given in the notes without careful proof: Let \(f:R \to S\) be a ring homomorphism. Let \(I\) be an ideal of \(R\) and let \(J\) be an ideal of \(S\). Then

\(I \subseteq I^{ec}\).
\(J^{ce} \subseteq J\).
\(I^{ece} = I^{e}\).
\(J^{cec} = J^c\).

Hint: You may assume if \(I_1 \subseteq I_2\) then \(I_1^e \subseteq I_2^e\) and similarly if \(J_1 \subseteq J_2\) then \(J_1^c \subseteq J_2^c\). You should be able to deduce 3&4 from 1&2.



Prove that the polynomial ring is a ring by proving the eight axioms. By far the hardest axiom is multiplicative associativity, which uses the convolutional multiplication rule twice.



The Eisenstein Integers \({\mathbb Z}[\omega] = \{x+y\omega | x, y \in {\mathbb Z}\}\) where \(\omega = \frac{\sqrt{-3}+1}{2}\). Notice that the angle of the complex number \(\omega\) is \(60^\circ\).
For this problem you may freely use the multiplicativity of complex norm: \(|wz| = |w||z|\) for all complex numbers \(w\), \(z\).

Sketch the set \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\) in the plane, including various positive and negative values of \(x\) and \(y\). You should get a regular lattice of points.
Let \(f:{\mathbb Z}[\omega] - \{0\} \to {\mathbb N}\) by \(f(a+bi) = a^2+b^2\). Calculate a formula for \(f(x+y\omega)\) in terms of \(x\) and \(y\).
Explain why \(f(r) \geq 1\) for elements of this ring.
Explain why \(f(rs) \geq f(r)\). The symmetric statement \(f(rs) \geq f(s)\) follows from commutativity.
What is the maximal distance between any point in the plane and the closest point on the lattice \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\)? Prove your answer geometrically.
Let \(a, b\) be nonzero elements of \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\). Let \(q = \left[\frac{b}{a}\right]\) and let \(r = b-qa\). The notation \([z]\) means “the closest Eisenstein integer to \(z\).” Prove that

\(b = qa+r\)
\(r=0\) or \(|r| < |a|\).


Conclude – what type of ring is \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\)?




Give an example of a PID \(R\) and subring \(S \subseteq R\) which is not a PID.




Give an example of a UFD \(R\) and a subring \(S \subseteq R\) which is not a UFD.
Give an example of a UFD \(R\) and a quotient ring \(R/I\) which is not a UFD.




Let \(a(x)\), \(b(x)\) be irreducible elements of \(K[x]\), neither a multiple of the other. Prove that there exist \(f(x)\), \(g(x)\) in \(K[x]\) so that \(f(x)a(x)+g(x)b(x)=1\). (This is a polynomial identity, not an identity for one value of \(x\).)

title: Homework Problems
text:
In this problem we explore the ring \(R = {\mathbb Z}[\sqrt{-5}] = \{a + b \sqrt{-5} | a, b \in {\mathbb Z}\}\).

Identify the \(0\) and \(1\) of \(R\). Prove (based on the definition above) that \(R\) is closed under addition and multiplication. Use the subring test to deduce that \(R\) is a subring of \({\mathbb C}\).
To describe the units of \(R\), we need something like a length function on it: For \(a+b\sqrt{-5} \in R\), we define \(\|a+b\sqrt{-5}\|^2 = a^2+5b^2\). (Note that this is just the complex square norm function restricted to \(R\).)


Explain why \(\| - \|^2\) is integer valued.
Prove that \(\Vert v \Vert^2\) is multiplicative in the sense \(\Vert vw\Vert^2 = \Vert v\Vert^2\Vert w\Vert^2\)
Prove (from the previous) that if \(v\) is a unit of \(R\), then \(\|v\|^2 = 1\).


Identify all units of \(R\).
Once units are identified, we can prove that certain elements are irreducible. Demonstrate that \(2\), \(3\), \(1+\sqrt{-5}\), and \(1-\sqrt{-5}\) are all irreducible.
It will perhaps bother you to see that \(2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5}) \cdot(1-\sqrt{-5})\). Among these irreducible factors of six, are any of them unit multiples of others? Why or why not?

title: Homework Problems
text:
Prove this proposition, which is given in the notes without careful proof: Let \(f:R \to S\) be a ring homomorphism. Let \(I\) be an ideal of \(R\) and let \(J\) be an ideal of \(S\). Then

\(I \subseteq I^{ec}\).
\(J^{ce} \subseteq J\).
\(I^{ece} = I^{e}\).
\(J^{cec} = J^c\).

Hint: You may assume if \(I_1 \subseteq I_2\) then \(I_1^e \subseteq I_2^e\) and similarly if \(J_1 \subseteq J_2\) then \(J_1^c \subseteq J_2^c\). You should be able to deduce 3&4 from 1&2.

title: Homework Problems
text:
The Eisenstein Integers \({\mathbb Z}[\omega] = \{x+y\omega | x, y \in {\mathbb Z}\}\) where \(\omega = \frac{\sqrt{-3}+1}{2}\). Notice that the angle of the complex number \(\omega\) is \(60^\circ\).
For this problem you may freely use the multiplicativity of complex norm: \(|wz| = |w||z|\) for all complex numbers \(w\), \(z\).

Sketch the set \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\) in the plane, including various positive and negative values of \(x\) and \(y\). You should get a regular lattice of points.
Let \(f:{\mathbb Z}[\omega] - \{0\} \to {\mathbb N}\) by \(f(a+bi) = a^2+b^2\). Calculate a formula for \(f(x+y\omega)\) in terms of \(x\) and \(y\).
Explain why \(f(r) \geq 1\) for elements of this ring.
Explain why \(f(rs) \geq f(r)\). The symmetric statement \(f(rs) \geq f(s)\) follows from commutativity.
What is the maximal distance between any point in the plane and the closest point on the lattice \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\)? Prove your answer geometrically.
Let \(a, b\) be nonzero elements of \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\). Let \(q = \left[\frac{b}{a}\right]\) and let \(r = b-qa\). The notation \([z]\) means “the closest Eisenstein integer to \(z\).” Prove that

\(b = qa+r\)
\(r=0\) or \(|r| < |a|\).


Conclude – what type of ring is \({\mathbb Z}[\omega]\)?

2 Course Information
Credit Hours: 3
Schedule: MWF 12:00-12:50, Carson 0208
Prerequisites: none
Required textbooks/materials: Openintro Statistics, Fourth Edition (An open textbook.)
Course Description: Elementary probabilistic and descriptive statistical concepts as applied to practical problems from other disciplines and an introduction to methods of statistical inference. Prerequisite: high school algebra or equivalent. Topics will include interpretation and analysis of data, calculation probabilities, calculation of mean, median, mode, standard deviation, and variance, fundamental counting principle, Central Limit Theorem, normal and binomial distributions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing.

title: Syllabus – 125
text:
3 Student Learning Objectives
Upon completion of this course, a student will

be able to distinguish between and a sample and population and then determine whether a numerical value is a statistic or parameter.
be able to calculate the mean, median, and mode for a data and decide which best represents the data set.
be able to calculate standard deviation and understand that the larger the standard deviation, the more varied the data values.
be able to determine whether or not two events are mutually exclusive.
know the Fundamental Counting Principle and whether or not an arrangement of objects is a permutation or combination and be able to count them.
know what a discrete and continuous random variables are.
recognize a normal distribution and be able to calculate probabilities using z-scores and tables or technology.
know the Central Limit Theorem and how to apply it and understand the standard deviation for the sampling distribution of sample means is less than that for the original distribution.
be able to construct confidence intervals for means and proportions and be able to interpret them.
be able to perform an hypothesis test for a mean using a normal or t-distribution and understand how to interpret the decision in the context of the problem.

5 Appendices

5.1 AI Policy:
Students are encouraged to leverage AI tools, such as Jupyter with code completion features or chatbots for learning help, to enhance their understanding of mathematical concepts and streamline computational tasks. All interactions with AI systems are consultations with an external source, just like a book or another person. Copying the work of an AI system and submitting it as ones own, even with some changes, is a form of plagiarism. Calling on AI for solutions to assigned problems is cheating, for the same reason that hiring your Mom to do your homework is cheating.


5.2 Thinking Mathematically:
Thinking Mathematically courses build proficiency with fundamental tools of mathematics, such as arithmetic, algebra, geometry, functions, graphs, and statistics. They teach students precise quantitative logical reasoning and applications of mathematical problem-solving skills in abstract and real-world problems. They engage students in oral and written communication of mathematical ideas.
Math 125 fulfills the Thinking Mathematically requirement of the Pathways Core Curriculum.

5.2.1 Thinking Mathematically Student Learning Outcomes:
At the conclusion of this course, students…

Use the fundamental tools of mathematics, such as arithmetic, algebra, geometry, functions, graphs, and statistics. (Applying)
Apply precise, logical quantitative reasoning to mathematical hypotheses and conditions. (Applying)
Identify mathematical structure and pattern. (Applying)
Engage in mathematical abstractions. (Applying)
Communicate effectively with oral and written skills appropriate to the discipline. (Understanding)



5.2.2 Methods of Instruction in relation to SLOs:
SLO #1: Students use boxplots, histograms, scatterplots, and other visualizations to analyze data sets. Students use arithmetic and algebra to construct confidence intervals and perform hypothesis testing. Students use functions and arithmetic to calculate descriptive statistics (mean, median, etc) of datasets. Students use statistics throughout the course.
SLO #2: Students solve verbal problems distinguishing between correlation and causation on homework and exams. They verify conditions such as near-normality and sample size for hypothesis tests. They answer homework questions on experiment design which require that they attend to the experimental conditions necessary to draw various conclusions.
SLO #3: Students learn to use basic data analysis techniques to discover patterns in data. The central limit theorem provides a recurring pattern which students use to solve problems involving p-values, including hypothesis testing, on homework and exams.
SLO #4: Students use the empirical rule to produce confidence intervals for individual data points and later for parameters based on inference. To understand the general formulations of these rules, students must think of datasets generically and abstractly. On most homeworks, students use formulas for statistics, tests, and inferences which are expressed abstractly to perform concrete computations. The notions of statistic and parameter are themselves abstractions of data computations.
SLO #5: Students discuss Statistics problems and their solutions in collaborative group work. They present solutions to their peers in the classroom. They also submit individual written work in the form of homework, quizzes, and exams.
SLO’s #1-#5 will be assessed on various homework problems.

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
2 One-sample test for proportion, overview
The parameter of interest is \(p\), a population proportion.
The statistic is \(\hat{p}\), a sample proportion.
The Alternative hypothesis is \(p > k\) or \(p < k\) or \(p \neq k\).
The Null hypothesis is \(p=k\)
The Standard Error is \(SE = \sqrt{\frac{k(1-k)}{n}}\).
The test statistic is \(Z = \frac{\hat{p}-k}{SE}\)

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
3 A hot day in Phoenix
Over the previous century (1911-2011), the proportion of days above 110°F in Phoenix, Arizona was 12/365. Consider this proportion a baseline for comparison. In the decade 2011-20, the proportion was 27/365. (Source, NOAA.) We wish to test whether the probability of a hot day now exceeds 12/365.

Is the data consistent with the hypothesis?
Find the standard error.
Find the Z-score of this measurement.
What is the p-value of this Z-score?
Is the difference likely due to chance?

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
4 A hot day in Phoenix (solution)

# Square root function needs import
from math import sqrt 

#Null hypothesis theory for p
p = 12/365

#Observed proportion
p2 = 27/365

# 10*365 days, plus leap days from '12, '16, '20)
n = 3653 

SE = sqrt(p*(1-p)/n) #Canned formula, using null value.

Z = (p2-p)/SE # (observed - predicted) / SE

# Import stats for "normal distribution" tool
from scipy import stats

# Find p-value as (left) tail area on normal distribution
pvalue = stats.norm.cdf(-Z)

print(Z)
print(pvalue)

13.929583127968339
2.0939634488594107e-44


The p-value is miniscule. The effect is not due to chance. The change is statistically significant.

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
5 Represent
About 50.5% of the US population is female (source: US Census). The US Senate (119th congress) has 26 women out of 100 senators (source: CAWP). We wish to test the theory that the US electoral system elects women with probability \(p < .505\).

Is the data consistent with the hypothesis?
Assume that senators’ genders are completely random (post-patriarchal utopia theory? \(p = .505\)), and calculate the standard error for such a sample.
Calculate the Z-score of the measurement \(26/100\).
Calculate a p-value for that Z-score. Is the discrepancy plausibly due to chance?

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
6 A biased coin 🪙
On game night, your friend always conducts coin flips with his “lucky coin,” a huge, heavy, American Silver Eagle. He’s lucky with it. You’re concerned that a coin might be biased. Working together, you perform an experiment with 1000 coin flips. He wins 525 of them.

Is the data consistent with the hypothesis?
Calculate the standard error for this experiment.
Calculate the Z-score of your result.
Calculate the p-value of the result.
Conclude: Is your friend busted for unfair play?

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
7 A lucky streak
In 2020, a gamer called Dream uploaded a world record Minecraft speedrun video. In it, Dream performed a certain randomized action (“trading for ender pearls”) 262 times, with success 42 times, a 16% success rate. Game logic dictates that success should be purely random (skill-independent) with a probability of 4.27%.

Is the data consistent with the hypothesis?
Calculate the standard error for this experiment.
Calculate the Z-score of Dream’s sample.
Calculate a p-value for that Z-score.
Is good luck a credible explanation for these events?

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
8 Z scores vs Z scores

Z score for the individual: (data value - mean) / σ Used to assess how out of whack one data value is, in relation to its distribution.
Z score for the experiment: (test statistic - null prediction) / SE Used to assess how strongly different from prediction is the experimental result.

title: 22. Hypothesis Testing – One Proportion
text:
9 Threshold of Significance

9.1 How small is small?
If \(p\) is small, we have a statistically significant result. If \(p\) is large, it’s inconclusive. How small is small?
\(\alpha = 0.05\) is a typical threshold of significance (or significance level). This is a social norm, which means it’s made up and can change.
\(\alpha = 0.005\) would be a better, stricter choice, requiring stronger evidence and producing fewer false positives results.
We must choose the threshold of significance before collecting data. Why?

title: 02. Association and Correlation

2 Vocabulary for relationships

Dependent / Associated / Correlated: Some statistical relationship exists
Positive Correlation: Higher x values linked to higher y values
Negative Correlation: Higher x values linked to lower y values
Independent: The variables are unrelated. No relationship exists.
Explanatory and Response variables: Variables causing an effect, or being effected, or expected to.
Correlation Coefficient \(\rho\): A numerical measurement of correlation. The output of df.corr()

title: 02. Association and Correlation

4 Correlation Coefficient
Just how correlated are two numerical variables?
The correlation coefficient \(\rho\) measures strength and direction of correlation.
Use df.corr(numeric_only=True) to calculate.
\(\rho\) nearly 1: x and y are strongly positively correlated.
\(\rho\) nearly 0: x and y are independent, at least not linearly correlated.
\(\rho\) nearly -1: x and y are strongly negatively correlated.
Correlations quickly flag trends and interrelationships for further study.

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
What is hypothesis testing?
A hypothesis is an idea or theory which can be tested.
Statistical evidence is evidence based on data. It’s usually subject to measurement error and sampling error.
A hypothesis test is a fair, objective procedure for weighing the strength of statistical evidence.
These procedures protect the integrity of science. They can’t remediate the effects of bad faith actors such as liars and tyrants.

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Why isn’t simple observation enough?

I’m concerned whether a coin is fair. I flipped it 100 times to check for bias. It landed heads 60 times. How do you interpret this evidence?
Does this drug lower blood pressure? In 30 patients on average bp went down 10 units. How strong is this evidence?

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Anatomy of a hypothesis test

Formulate hypothesis. Make it a testable, numerical statement of difference.
Collect data. Avoid bias.
Is the data consistent with hypothesis?

If no, announce no evidence.
If yes, is the measured effect plausibly due to chance?

if yes, announce inconclusive result.

if no, announce statistically significant result



3b is the tricky bit. It requires the probability, if the hypothesis were wrong, of finding the effect from chance measurement error.

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Hypothesis test, simple example
In the 2012 World Series, the San Francisco Giants swept the Detroit Tigers (4-0) by winning four games in a row. Which statements best support the claim that the Giants were a better team?

Hypothesis: In any given game, \(P(\text{ Giants win }) > .5\)
The 4-0 sweep is the data.
Is the data consistent with hypothesis? Yes
Is the effect plausibly due to chance? If they were only equally good, \(P(\text{ four wins }) = 1/16 \approx 6\%\). Yes, the result is plausibly due to chance.

Verdict: Inconclusive
(Note: The number \(1/16\) is the p-value of the test. See below.)

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Hypothesis test, second example
You suspect a die is rigged not to roll “1”.

Hypothesis: \(P(\text{ landing 1 }) < 1/6\)
The evidence: Out of 30 rolls, the die never lands “1”.
Is the data consistent with hypothesis? Yes
Is the effect plausibly due to chance? The chance of no 1’s out of 30 rolls on a fair die is \((5/6)^{30} = 0.00421\). No, the result is not plausibly due to chance.

Verdict: Statistically Significant Evidence. The die is unfair.
(Note: The number \(.00421\) is the p-value of the test. See below.)

section: Changing an idea into a hypothesis

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Notes on hypothesis statements
A good hypothesis statement should:

Assert a difference or inequality.
Refer to parameters, not statistics.

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Typical hypotheses

Compare mean to baseline: \(\mu >10\)
Compare two means \(\mu_1 > \mu_2\).
Compare proportion to baseline: \(p > 0.5\)
Compare two proportions: \(p_m > p_w\).

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
Two-sided hypotheses
A two-sided hypothesis states a difference but doesn’t say which way. Both high and low evidence can support a two-sided hypothesis.

\(\mu \neq 10\)
\(\mu_1 \neq \mu_2\).
\(p \neq 0.5\)
\(p_m \neq p_w\).

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
The Counterpoint – Null Hypothesis



Hypothesis \(H_A\)
Null Hypothesis \(H_0\)




Global temps are rising
Global temps are constant


Managers biased vs. women
Managers are fair


\(\mu > 0.75\)
\(\mu = 0.75\)


\(p_A > p_B\)
\(p_A = p_B\)



The job of the Null Hypothesis is to assert no difference, not to reverse the difference.
When we ask “Is the effect plausibly due to chance?” we mean in a world where the Null Hypothesis were true.

title: 21. Introduction to Statistical Hypotheses
text:
P-value and threshold
A hypothesis test hinges on the plausibility that our results are due to chance.
We need the probability, in a Null Hypothesis world, of getting results as strong as those witnessed. This probability is called the p-value. If the p-value is large, the results are plausibly due to chance. If the p-value is small, the results are not due to chance and so are statistically significant.
The cut-off between “large” and “small” p-values is often chosen to be \(0.05\), and this choice is called the threshold of significance.

2 Three explanations for correlation (at least!)


For each scenario, which is more likely? Why?

A influences B (directly or indirectly)
B influences A (directly or indirectly)
Some lurking variable is driving both A and B.



Daily ice cream sales and gasoline sales are significantly correlated.
Social media use and depression are correlated.
In school children, finger length and reading ability are strongly correlated.
Both caffeinated soda use and ADHD diagnoses have increased in children over the last 20 years.

title: 03. Correlation is not Causation
text:
3 Start with an open mind.
Cultivate creative skepticism and critical thinking.
Athletes with high PPG (points per game) have higher GPA (grade point average).
Give three credible explanations based on the three forms of the previous slide. Brainstorming all three explanation types!

title: 03. Correlation is not Causation
text:
4 Lurking (“Confounding”) variables
Any variable, often unmeasured, that drives a correlation between two other variables. When discovered, lurking variables tend to explain away apparent relationships between other variables.

Coffee consumption and lung cancer are positively correlated. (Really!) We should not conclude that coffee causes lung cancer. There may be lurking variables which we have not considered. One of the hallmarks of critical thinking is not jumping to conclusions.

title: 03. Correlation is not Causation
text:
5 So… withhold judgment forever?

Attendance rate is correlated to class grade.
Laws against trans people are associated to violence against trans people.
Within certain banks, loan acceptance is associated to applicant race.
Cigarette smoking is correlated to lung cancer.

The idea of confounding variables can become a hater’s new excuse to dismiss statistical evidence. In cases where common sense understanding, historical understanding, or controlled experimental support a conclusion, we can’t just wave it away!

title: 03. Correlation is not Causation
section: 6 In an age of industrialized, weaponized, Grade-A propaganda, how do I know who or what to believe?
text:
6 In an age of industrialized, weaponized, Grade-A propaganda, how do I know who or what to believe?
Yikes. I’m no oracle! These simple rules have served me well.

Study history. What’s past is prologue.
The truth is often complicated. Get comfortable with nuance and be suspicious of those with none.
“When someone shows you who they are, believe them the first time.” –Maya Angelou
If the Nazis are on your side, you’re on the wrong side.

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
text:
7 Technical definition, for the record
Technically, normal is not just unimodal, symmetric, unskewed, and bell shaped. A normal distribution fits the specific formula below. Lucky for us, we don’t need to use or memorize the formula in Math 125!
\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\]

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
text:
8 Central Limit Theorem

8.1 When should we expect a distribution to be normal?
If a data variable aggregates many small independent effects, it’s usually normal or close. For example:

Human height (arguably)
Exam scores (usually)
Cholesterol levels (usually)
Game scores in sports (basketball more than hockey!)
Sampling distributions (This is foreshadowing. More on this later!)

This phenomenon is called the Central Limit Theorem. Its precise statement is too technical for Math 125.

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
text:
11 The empirical rule (68-95-99.7)

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm

# Parameters for the normal distribution
mu = 0  # Mean
sigma = 1  # Standard deviation

# Generate data for the normal distribution curve
x = np.linspace(mu - 4*sigma, mu + 4*sigma, 500)
y = norm.pdf(x, mu, sigma)

# Calculate exact percentages using CDF
percent_1std = (norm.cdf(sigma) - norm.cdf(-sigma)) * 100
percent_2std = (norm.cdf(2*sigma) - norm.cdf(-2*sigma)) * 100
percent_3std = (norm.cdf(3*sigma) - norm.cdf(-3*sigma)) * 100

# Create the plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
ax.plot(x, y, color='blue', linewidth=2, label='Normal Distribution PDF')

# Mark the mean
ax.axvline(mu, color='black', linestyle='--', label=r'Mean ($\mu$) = 0')

# Define the standard deviation ranges
std1_left, std1_right = mu - sigma, mu + sigma
std2_left, std2_right = mu - 2*sigma, mu + 2*sigma
std3_left, std3_right = mu - 3*sigma, mu + 3*sigma

# Shade the areas for 68%, 95%, and 99.7%
# 99.7% (3 standard deviations)
x_fill_3std = x[(x >= std3_left) & (x <= std3_right)]
y_fill_3std = y[(x >= std3_left) & (x <= std3_right)]
ax.fill_between(x_fill_3std, 0, y_fill_3std, color='purple', alpha=0.1, label=f'$\mu \pm 3\sigma$ ({percent_3std:.2f}%)')

# 95% (2 standard deviations)
x_fill_2std = x[(x >= std2_left) & (x <= std2_right)]
y_fill_2std = y[(x >= std2_left) & (x <= std2_right)]
ax.fill_between(x_fill_2std, 0, y_fill_2std, color='green', alpha=0.2, label=f'$\mu \pm 2\sigma$ ({percent_2std:.2f}%)')

# 68% (1 standard deviation)
x_fill_1std = x[(x >= std1_left) & (x <= std1_right)]
y_fill_1std = y[(x >= std1_left) & (x <= std1_right)]
ax.fill_between(x_fill_1std, 0, y_fill_1std, color='red', alpha=0.3, label=f'$\mu \pm 1\sigma$ ({percent_1std:.2f}%)')

# Add labels for standard deviation marks
plt.text(mu + sigma, norm.pdf(mu + sigma, mu, sigma) + 0.02, r'$\mu + \sigma$', horizontalalignment='center', color='red')
plt.text(mu - sigma, norm.pdf(mu - sigma, mu, sigma) + 0.02, r'$\mu - \sigma$', horizontalalignment='center', color='red')
plt.text(mu + 2*sigma, norm.pdf(mu + 2*sigma, mu, sigma) + 0.02, r'$\mu + 2\sigma$', horizontalalignment='center', color='green')
plt.text(mu - 2*sigma, norm.pdf(mu - 2*sigma, mu, sigma) + 0.02, r'$\mu - 2\sigma$', horizontalalignment='center', color='green')
plt.text(mu + 3*sigma, norm.pdf(mu + 3*sigma, mu, sigma) + 0.02, r'$\mu + 3\sigma$', horizontalalignment='center', color='purple')
plt.text(mu - 3*sigma, norm.pdf(mu - 3*sigma, mu, sigma) + 0.02, r'$\mu - 3\sigma$', horizontalalignment='center', color='purple')

# Set title and labels
ax.set_title('Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7) Illustration', fontsize=16)
ax.set_xlabel('Standard Deviations above/below the mean', fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel('Probability Density', fontsize=12)
ax.legend(loc='upper right')
ax.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
section: 17 A fair rating – data in context
text:
17 A fair rating – data in context
Judge relative to average – subtract \(\mu\).
Judge relative to variability – divide by \(\sigma\).
\[\text{Z-score} = \frac{\text{data value} - \mu}{\sigma}\]
Z-score = number of standard deviations from the mean.
Z-score is an interchangeable standard of unusualness, scaled to the distribution the data belongs to.

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
text:
18 Intuition for Z-scores
It counts the number of standard deviations from the mean, which is a statistically “fair” across different distributions.

Z = 0: Average.
Z = +1, -1: Uninteresting.
Z = +2, -2: Raise eyebrow.
Z = +3, -3: Remarkable.
Z = +5, -5: Stunning.

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
text:
19 Practice with Z score

A distribution for test scores is normally distributed \(N(500, 50^2)\). You score 625. Well done! What is your Z score?
An LED manufacture process produces units with illumination \(N(50,0.2^2)\). One particular bulb has illumination 49.4.


What is its Z-score?
If we reject any bulb at 49.4 or below, how much of the inventory would we waste?
By reconfiguring the assembly process, we can make the distribution \(N(51, 1^2)\). How would you describe the effect of this change? How would this affect the manufacturing waste?

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
section: 20 The rarity of a Z-score: the p-value
text:
20 The rarity of a Z-score: the p-value
A good measure of the unusualness of a Z-score is the portion of the curve at least as extreme as that score, called the \(p\)-value.

20.1 Use Bognar’s tool to answer:

How much of the normal distribution is above Z = 2.3?
How much of the normal distribution is more extreme, on either side, than Z=3.1?



20.2 Use stats.norm.cdf to answer:

How much of the normal distribution is below Z = -5?
How much of the normal distribution is above Z = 2.5?

title: 18-19. The Normal Distribution
text:
21 Putting it all together

Most people tend to score about 550 on a given exam, with a standard deviation of 60. Your score is 685. Good job! What is your Z-score? What is your percentile?
An average business day sees about $1000 in sales, with a standard deviation of about $200. Sales were slow today. Only $450. What is the Z-score? How rare is such a disastrous sales day?
A 1000-letter sample of English language should have on average about 80 “a”’s, with a standard deviation of about 9. A randomly chosen Youtube video description has 1000 characters but 120 “a”’s. What is the Z-score of this result? How rare is it? Can you think of alternate explanations?

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
section: Correct each statement – statistics vs. parameters.
text:
Correct each statement – statistics vs. parameters.

I sampled 500 patients and averaged their blood pressure. Now I know the population average blood pressure.
I surveyed 500 teens and calculated a bullying risk probability. Now I know a parameter.
I sampled 500 library books. Now I know the average length of all books.
I weighed 500 cats. Now I know μ, the average weight of cats.

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
The problem

Statistical measurements only estimate parameters. When a statistic is used to estimate a parameter, we call it a point estimate.
Statistical measurement error is natural and inevitable. Point estimates naturally differ from the parameters they intend to measure.

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
The compensation

Large samples allow us to limit measurement error.
Special formulas (for SE) allow us to quantify and predict measurement error.
Confidence intervals allow us to responsibly report our point estimates and their potential error in a responsible way.

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
The good news

Usually, measurement error is not just random, but normal N(0,…) with mean 0 and predictable deviation.
The deviation of the error of a point estimate is called the Standard Error (SE).

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Visualizing Standard Error
Adjust the sliders to see how the sample size (\(n\)) and the number of resamples (\(m\)) affect the distribution of the mean.

Set \(n=25\). When \(m=1\), what happens? Why is the single red dot close to \(10\)? Why isn’t it exactly at \(10\)? Why isn’t it at the same place as on your neighbor’s screen?
Raise \(m\). Why are the red dots close to \(10\)? Why do they vary? How much do they stray from \(10\), typically? That’s Standard Error
Keeping \(m\) somewhat large, Raise \(n\). Do the red dots spread out farther from \(10\) or cluster more closely? Has standard error gone up or down?
With large \(m\), set \(n=1\). Why does the right-hand plot look like that?
The original population is quite skewed. For large \(n\), is the sampling distribution skewed or normal?

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
text:
Three huge takeaways.

The Standard Error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution. It depends on the deviation in the original population and also depends on \(n\).
Large-sample (i.e. big n) averages cluster tightly around the true mean. This is the Law of Large Numbers.
Regardless of the shape of the original distribution, large-sample averages follow a normal bell curve. This is the Central Limit Theorem. The bell curve’s mean and variability are described in parts 1 & 2 above.

title: 20. Standard Error and Confidence Intervals
section: SE as the basis for Confidence Intervals
text:
SE as the basis for Confidence Intervals
You have a point estimate for a parameter. It approximates a parameter. You want to guess the parameter.
The Empirical Rule says that 95% of the time, the measurement error is less than \(2*SE\), so the confidence interval: \[\text{ point estimate } \pm 2*SE\] almost certainly captures the parameter.

title: 24. Hypothesis Testing – One Mean
text:
The parameter of interest is \(\mu\), a population mean.
The statistic is \(\bar{x}\), a sample mean.
The alternative hypothesis is \(\mu > k\) or \(\mu < k\) or \(\mu \neq k\).
The null hypothesis is \(\mu=k\)
The standard error is \(SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)
The test statistic is \(t = \frac{\bar{x}-k}{SE}\)

title: 24. Hypothesis Testing – One Mean
text:
The parameter of interest is \(\mu\), a population mean.
The statistic is \(\bar{x}\), a sample mean.
The alternative hypothesis is \(\mu > k\) or \(\mu < k\) or \(\mu \neq k\).
The null hypothesis is \(\mu=k\)
The standard error is \(SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)
The test statistic is \(t = \frac{\bar{x}-k}{SE}\)

title: 24. Hypothesis Testing – One Mean
text:
2 The T-test, an added wrinkle


The standard error in this case “should be” \(SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), but we almost never know \(\sigma\). The sample stdev \(s\) is what we know, and it’s close.
The \(Z\)-score \(Z = \frac{\bar{x}-k}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}\) would be a normally distributed estimation error but our substitute \(t = \frac{\bar{x}-k}{s / \sqrt{n}}\) is not, because the denominator is subtly data-dependent.
We shouldn’t compare a t-score to the normal distribution. We must use a “modified normal” distribution called a t-distribution, which accounts for the problem \(s \neq \sigma\).
The “fix” depends on sample size. The \(t\)-distribution with \(n-1\) “degrees of freedom” is the right one.

title: 24. Hypothesis Testing – One Mean
text:
3 Identifying a t-test.
A restaurant supplier predicts delivery of salmon fillets with an average mass of 600 grams. This week’s average is only 580 with a standard deviation of 30 (n=100). This is smaller than the agreed average size. Is this statistically significantly smaller?

A mean (not a proportion) is compared.
There is a hypothesis to check comparing the mean to baseline or another mean.
We have a standard deviation from the dataset but no population standard deviation.

title: 24. Hypothesis Testing – One Mean
text:
4 Example 1 – a fishy discrepancy
A restaurant supplier predicts delivery of salmon fillets with an average mass of 600 grams. This week’s average is only 580 with a standard deviation of 30 (n=100). This is smaller than the agreed average size. Is this statistically significantly smaller?

# Square root function needs import
from math import sqrt 

#Record givens
k = 600  # Null hypothesis theory
x = 580  # Observed mean
n = 100  # sample size
s = 30   # SAMPLE standard deviation.

SE = s / sqrt(n) 
t = (x - k)/SE # (observed - predicted) / SE

# Import stats for "t distribution" tool, not normal!
from scipy import stats

# Find p-value as (left) tail area on t distribution
pvalue = stats.t.cdf(t, 99) 
# Note t was negative so I didn't negate it.

print(t)
print(pvalue)

7.50614450498516e-10
